Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works)1: On June 9 two hon. members of the house complained of traffic conditions on parliament hill. The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) put the following question:
I wish to ask the Minister of Public Works if something cannot be done to stop cars from speeding around the parliament buildings and on the roads leading to the gates of the parliament buildings.
The leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Cold-well) added this:
May I ask the Minister of Public Works if he will at the same time take into consideration the strengthening of the hands of the mounted police who look after the automobiles around this building.
At that time I replied that some doubt had been raised as to the authority of the mounted police to enforce these regulations, and said I would submit this question to the justice department. The question was studied by the Department of Justice and yesterday I received their opinion, which reads as follows:
With reference to the act to provide for the regulation of vehicular traffic on dominion property. I have come to the conclusion and so advise that this extends and applies to the roadways situated on parliament hill. An examination of the authorities persuades me now that the courts would be obliged to hold that these roadways have not been dedicated as public highways. Consequently it is not necessary to amend the statute.
Following this advice I may state that it is the intention of the government to enforce these regulations. We hope all hon. members and officials of the government will cooperate with the police so they may carry out their duties. We have had quite a bit of trouble in the last two or three months, but I hope this announcement that we will enforce these regulations will reestablish satisfactory conditions on the hill.

subtopic: GENERAL REVISION APPLICABLE TO 1948 AND SUBSEQUENT TAXATION YEARS

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 454, respecting income taxes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in my budget speech some weeks ago I expressed the hope that I would be able to place before the house this session a revision of the income tax law.
It is, perhaps, unnecessary for me to repeat that it is not the intention of the government to press this bill for enactment at the present session. Nor, indeed, is it my wish to invite debate on the measure at this time. The purpose of introducing the bill now is to give members full opportunity to study it before next session, to explore thoroughly various aspects of the legislation, and to be in a position to give parliament the benefit of their views when the bill is presented for enactment next session.
It is hoped that this bill will receive wide circulation in the hands of the public. Various organizations throughout the country, such as the Canadian Bar Association, the Dominion Association of Chartered Accountants, and the Canadian Tax Foundation, are well equipped from the technical point of view to render a useful service to the country through an exhaustive analysis of this legislation. I can assure all interested groups that suggestions for improvement in the statute will be welcomed and given careful study by the government.
A bill of this kind is, of course, definitely non-political. I think all parties agree that we must have an income tax. We are unanimous in our desire to see the best possible law on our statute books. All agree that we should strive for simplicity and certainty. The law should lend itself to efficient administration. We are, I think, all on common ground in seeking these objectives. Once the best possible instrument has been forged, it then, of course, becomes a political matter as to how far the instrument will be used as a revenue measure and how the total burden imposed by it will be distributed among taxpayers.
It is not my intention to delay the business of the house at this time with a detailed account of how the new bill differs from the present Act. I think, however, it might be helpful if I briefly indicated the general plan of the revision, giving some of the highlights of the new measure, and pointing out certain methods used to secure greater simplicity and directness. To assist in getting a picture of the new arrangement of the law I have had

Income Tax Act
a comprehensive table of contents prepared and inserted at the beginning of the bill. Also, in addition to marginal notes opposite each section or subsection, members will find on each right-hand page references to the corresponding provisions in the present law. This will readily enable comparisons to be made between present and proposed legislation.
The bill divides the subject matter into eight parts as compared with eighteen parts in the present Act. Part 1 covers the general income tax on individuals and corporations which, of course, is the main body of the law. Part 2 imposes the taxes on non-residents, which taxes are deducted at the source on payments leaving Canada. These two parts cover the fundamental part of the taxing statute. The content of the remaining parts can easily be determined by running through the various headings.
As I have stated, part 1 deals with income tax proper, and it is set up under eight divisions. It will be seen the bill starts off directly with what is known as the charging section. It commences by stating who is liable for tax. This direct way of starting a piece of legislation of this kind may be regarded by the house as a perfectly obvious and logical way to open such a statute. However, under the present law the charging section is not reached until thirty-eight pages of other material have been presented.
Perhaps the house would bear with me if I read section 2 of the bill, because I think it offers a fair sample of the simplicity of language and the directness of the approach in the new law which have been among the main objectives in the revision.
2. (1) An income tax shall be paid as hereinafter required upon the taxable income for each taxation year of every person resident in Canada at any time an the year.
(2)	Where a person who is not taxable under subsection one for a taxation year
(a)	was employed in Canada in performing the duties of an office or employment at any time in fhe year, or
(b)	carried on business in Canada at any time in the year,
an income tax shall be paid as hereinafter required upon the part of his taxable income for the year that was earned in Canada
(3)	The taxable income of a taxpayer for a taxation year is bis income for the year minus the deductions permitted by division III.
Division II starts in by giving general rules for computing income. I should perhaps mention here that after exhaustive study of the legislation of other countries and of the nature of the problems involved, it was decided not to attempt a specific definition of income. So far as I know, no country has achieved a satisfactory definition. Accordingly, the general scheme of the law, as will be seen by section 3 is to tax jdl income and to indicate the general sources of income, that is, income from businesses, property and offices or employments. Section 4 follows up this general indication by stating that income from a business or property shall be determined in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. We believe that by providing a general formula of this kind the best practical common sense results will be achieved. The income tax division in making assessments will interpret the legislation and the taxpayer, if he disagrees, may have his case heard by the new income tax appeal board and, if still not satisfied, take it to the exchequer court.
I should like to call particular attention to division VIII at the end of part I. The house will observe that it provides for what might be called a set of boxes for exceptional kinds of taxpayers or special provisions not of general application. In the previous law these items cluttered up the main body of the law. A separate division for these unusual cases or situations greatly simplifies the part of the statute which is of general interest to the ordinary taxpayer.
Special attention has been given in this revision to the question of ministerial discretion. The house may recall that the income tax legislation of last year provided for an ad>-visory board to review cases where ministerial discretion had been exercised under forty-three designated provisions in the law. The house may be interested to know that of these forty-three ministerial discretions only two remain in the new bill. Furthermore, these remaining two do not affect the amount of any tax payable. One requires the concurrence of the minister upon the change of a fiscal period of a taxpayer, and the other gives the minister power to determine who shall be the taxpayer where multiple trusts are set up in favour of the same beneficiary.
In cases where some degree of flexibility is felt necessary we provide that rules shall be determined by regulations fixed by order in council, which will be subject to review by the courts and will not involve the objectionable principle of ministerial discretion, as is the case in the existing law.
Possibly the house would be interested in the method adopted in eliminating discretions. This has been done by converting the discretion into a rule of law dependent on a question of fact. An example will make this clear. For instance, subsection 2 of section 6 in the present law states that
the minister may disallow any expense which he in his discretion may determine to be in excess of what is reasonable or normal for the business carried on by the taxpayer...
Income Tax Act

The corresponding provision in the bill provides that ,
Where a disbursement or expense or a part thereof is otherwise deductible, only such part thereof as is reasonable in the circumstances may be deducted in computing income.
In practice the department in making an assessment may disallow a certain portion of an item of expense as being unreasonable in the circumstances. If the taxpayer is dissatisfied with hke assessment on the basis used by the department he can appeal the assessment and the mew income tax appeal board will pass judgment on the case, that is, the court will decide whether the department has acted reasonably. The government is prepared to give this system a thorough trial. It may be found, however, that certain discretions may have to be reinstated if experience shows that the subject matter is not appropriate to judicial determination.
In view of the extent to which ministerial discretions have been removed from the law, it will now be unnecessary to proceed with the appointment of the income tax advisory board provided for in last year's legislation. I shall recommend, therefore, a.t the next session of parliament that the authority for this board and for appeals from ministerial discretion be repealed ab initio.
I trust the house will pardon me if upon this occasion I express a certain pride in the work that has been accomplished in this revision of our income tax law. I should not, however, like to give the house the impression that I think this bill is by any means perfect. As a matter of fact I remain open-minded on some of-the changes in the new bill. It is probable that further study will require further changes. I should also like to make it clear that because of pressure on my time some important questions have not been finally settled. I quite realize, for example, that the various penalty provisions need careful examination. Some of these outstanding items will be dealt with later when the legislation is introduced for enactment in the 1948 session of parliament. In the- -meantime further consideration is being given to them. It would be my thought that when the bill is introduced in 1948 to make it retroactive to January 1st of that year.
An attempt has been made by the translators to have the translation into French follow closely with the original drafting in English. I find, however, that the numerous last-minute changes in the draft have not yet fully been dealt with by the translators, with the result that -a few days may elapse before the French text of the bill is available. I am sorry about this, but I am assured that the copies in French will be available for circulation shortly.

I should not like to close this statement without saying a few words about the officials who to a great extent are responsible for the work embodied- in this bill. Over the past year senior officials of the departments of justice, finance- and national revenue have, in addition to their regular work, devoted an incredible amount of time and effort to this revision. It has meant a great deal of night work and sacrifice of leisure. Unless a person has had some experience in attempting to revise an exceedingly complex statute of this kind he can have no idea of the difficulties involved in re-writing such a law. I have personally taken a great interest in the work, and speaking from my close association with the officials in this matter I wanted publicity to express appreciation to them for their excellent work.

Mr. Speaker, for obvious reasons I shall make only brief comments on two things. I think we are all g-lad to know that this long overdue measure is now-not before us, but in sight of being before us for action. I do not propose to say anything more except that in the first budget speech I heard in this house, which was nearly two years ago, the Minister of Finance referred to this measure and said it was overdue. It was certainly overdue and I regret the time that has elapsed since without any general revision of the act. However, that is past.
Just a comment on what the minister has said. If this bill is successful, as the minister indicated, in introducing simplicity of language and directness of approach, then certainly the minister is entitled to the pride which he says he has in it. I was glad that he referred to his openmindedness, although with legal caution he qualified that by saying that he could not be expected to be open-minded on all questions.
I am sure we all agree that- we owe a debt to those civil servants who have worked on this and who have produced, in its first stage at any rate, a measure which has been so long needed.

___________Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Atomic energy control board-
355. Administration expenses, $115,000.

Just yesterday we received the first annual report of this board, which was authorized by a special act last session. There is a large increase over last year's figure for administration expenses which I should like the minister to explain. The minister will remember that during the debate last year there was some discussion as to whether it would be a full-time board or a part-time board, and apparently the decision has been reached that the board will act only on a part-time basis.
According to page 3 of the report the board has held only five meetings since it was set up. Meetings were held on October 16, 17 and 18, 1946; one was held on January 6, 1947, and a final meeting is shown here as having been held on March 15, 1946, but I presume that should be March 15, 1947. This board was given the most drastic powers that have ever been given to a board by any Canadian government. In addition to that, parliament was told: Hands off; the atomic energy control board must not be interfered with by a parliamentary committee; there is to be "no check at all of any kind; the board is supreme." The picture we have today is that this part-time board in effect has met only three times since it was set up, because the first three meetings were on consecutive dates. The members of that board are engaged on other duties; I believe that General McNaughton, the chairman, spends a great deal of his time at the united nations meetings, and quite properly so-
Or on atomic energy business.

The time has come when there should be some watchdog committee of the Senate and House of Commons with respect to atomic energy. We have been told by the minister that Canada is concerned only with the production of atomic energy for peacetime purposes, and that is another very good reason why there should be no hesitation in giving parliament some check over the matter. I do urge, as I did1 last year, that there should be some parliamentary check. This House of Commons, representing the people of Canada, is entitled to have a hand in the control of atomic energy developments. It is a thoroughly bad principle to give these very drastic powers to a board which is not
under control of the house, particularly a part-time board which is doing this work only as a sideline. The minister said last night that the operations at Chalk River were being carried on not by this board but by the national research council. I think the time has come, Mr. Chairman, when some effective method of control should be given to parliament.

The board was intended to be a part-time board except for the chairman, who is on full-time duty. Unfortunately his paramount duty in connection with atomic energy has been to represent Canada on the atomic energy panel of the united nations. General McNaughton has been in almost continuous session on that panel. He has been chairman of it from time to time and has been a very active member.
One reason why the expenditure will be larger next year is that when General McNaughton was appointed, chairman he was on the payroll of external affairs, and that is stiill the situation. His salary was not charged to the atomic energy board during the past fiscal year.
The members of the board, while they have not met together formally, have been very active on atomic energy work. Dean Mackenzie spends a good portion of his time at Chalk River and is engaged in matters having to do with the work of the board. My own deputy minister, who is also a member of the board, has visited Chalk River frequently and has devoted a great deal of his time to the board. The same applies to the other members. Mr. Bateman has been very active on the raw materials procurement side. To form a judgment of the board on the number of meetings it has held in its initial stages would be fallacious. Another factor to be taken into account is that one of the principal duties of the board is to deal with products and bv-products of the plant at Chalk River. It takes some months to recover those by-products, and therefore the problem of disposing of them has not become an active problem as yet, although it will so become before the end of this calendar year.
The board has carried out the duties given to it by parliament and has carefully protected the raw materials which are produced in this country. There again that task has been simple because only one company is producing the raw materials and that company is government-owned. I have no doubt however that production by private interests will appear and the production of raw materials will require control by the board,. I suggest that everything is under control. My

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply______
hon. friend has said that since they are producing the products for peace-time uses only, there should be no secrecy.
} did not say that.

He suggested control by a parliamentary committee or something of the sort. I would point out that the material is the same material whether it is used for purposes of peace or war purposes. The fact that we now use it for peace-time purposes would not prevent this government or anybody else from using it for war purposes. It is just as explosive as the material that other people make for war purposes. Therefore the same secrecy provisions must be maintained; in fact, they have been tightened over the past year. In taking that precaution we are following the procedure of all governments manufacturing or dealing with this commodity.

The minister is not following the procedure in the United States so far as parliamentary control is concerned, because there they do have a watchdog committee of the Senate and House of Representatives. The minister said last year that he thought such a committee in Canada would be feasible eventually, but he was not prepared to recommend it last year. Has the time not come when such a committee could be set up?

I think not. Atomic energy is such an explosive subject at the moment- it is under discussion at Lake Success and in the newspapers-that my thought is that the best contribution Canada can make for the next year is to avoid any discussion of atomic energy. I think that is the wise course to take. I read the proceedings of the Senate committee and so far as Canada is concerned there would be no objection to giving the same information to a committee about the Canadian project as was given about the United States project, but I think no good purpose would be served by doing so. Therefore I suggest that the matter be allowed to stand as it is for another year, and that, at the next session I shall be glad to review the position and discuss the establishment of a committee of the house or the Senate to meet in camera and examine the officials of the atomic energy board.

I would point out to the minister that my thought is not that a committee should be told secrets that nobody else is allowed to get, but rather that there should be a body of parliamentarians who are studying the implications of this new power, atomic energy. I think it is agreed on all sides that atomic energy is going to make

vast changes in our whole economy, yet here we are in the Senate and House of Commons with no one but the minister understanding anything about the development of atomic energy. Canada is in the forefront, one of the three leaders in the development of atomic energy, and yet we are not taking any steps to build up an informed opinion among the people who are responsible for leading the nation. I think that is a very unsound position for this government to take. I would not ask that such a committee be told secrets that should be carefully kept-not at all. But I do suggest that there would be great value in having somebody here study the whole question, and I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to arranging that such a committee or some similar body be set up at the next session.

I shall be glad to keep that suggestion in mind and will do so at the first opportune moment, Canada is one of the two nations of the world which are producing this material. The paramount consideration at the moment is that the secrecy provision be preserved, and I am sure my hon. friend will agree with that position.

The hon. member for Vancouver South has made it very clear that he agrees with that. He was very specific indeed, but so far as I am concerned the minister has not satisfied me that this indefinite delay in setting up a discreet and limited committee, if you like, which the hon. member for Vancouver South suggested, is justified. Nothing that the minister has said is an answer to that request. I hope that he will take it in mind very seriously, because at the present time what is being said to us in this house in effect is that we are a lot of children who cannot be persuaded to behave like grown men. That is the position in which we are. We recognize, and my hon. friend has made it clear, the position that the minister is in. We respect that and we want to protect it. We do not want him to tell us things we should not know. My hon. friend has made that clear, but there is surely a middle ground between that and this house and the other house being in effect told that they might as well not ask any questions but be good little boys. I hope the minister will take that seriously under review. I can see no reason for the delay.
There is one other point I should like to mention. This item covers $115,000 for administration expenses. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but there are no details. Is that right?

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I think that is right, yes.

Why should we not have more details? No secrets are connected with this item. We know the salaries that are being paid to most important civil servants. Why do we have to take it sight unseen, as they say in the street? I am dealing with what the minister said a moment ago, that he would not give details. If I am wrong the minister will correct me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Turn to page 214.

I still think my hon. friend has not answered the question. The explanation on page 214 says, "Temporary assistance, S75,000." That means that we are not to have any knowledge as to what is being paid to other people. I cannot see at all that that is a secret which goes to the root of security. It is not clear to me why we should be asked to pass these omnibus items and know nothing about payments which are being made to people merely because they are not on the permanent civil service list.

There is no objection to giving the salaries of the personnel. The salaries of the staff last year, outside of salaries to the members, because none were paid last year, are as follows. The salaries of government staff $8,936.21 for the period from October 12 to March 31, which is the period that the board functioned; temporary salaries $1,250. making a total of $10,186.21. There is an item of $25.73 for special temporary assistance; travelling expenses $1,325.54; printing and stationery $685.90.
I am not asking the minister to give all these details; I am just asking for the main items of salaries, if he would care to give them. I do not want to waste the time of the committee.

I am sorry; I cannot give
the salaries because I have not the details at hand. I can send for them if the hon. member is interested. There is no objection to giving this; but in reply to the remarks that have been made I might point out that General McNaughton, the chairman of the board, appeared before the external affairs committee of the House of Commons. He was examined there and gave all the information that in the opinion of the government could be given publicly. My hon. friend will appreciate that. There is no desire to withhold information that can properly be given; but in talking of the process it is very difficult to be able to
sort out information that can be given and information that cannot be given. One slip in information that cannot be given brings instant criticism from the others who share this process with us. I am simply asking for another year to consider the position as to what machinery can be set up as a means of communication between the board and parliament.

The minister would not
suggest for a moment that the fact that General McNaughton appeared before the external affairs committee and made a statement which had to do primarily with the international implications is an answer to my criticism that there should be some committee of parliament studying this question. I am on the external affairs committee, and this is only one of the sidelines. Incidentally, they do not pretend to be specialists on atomic energy.

I am simply suggesting the fact that General McNaughton did appear before the committee is an indication that there is no desire on the part of the government to withhold from parliament any information that can properly be given.

The
whole problem of atomic energy is of great concern to every parliamentarian and to the Canadian people generally. I recognize that at this late hour in the session we do not desire a full-dress debate on the subject. I remember that in the first session of this parliament the whole post-war problem of what we were going to do with atomic energy was thrown in our laps. In all deference to the lack of knowledge which hon. members have in that regard, I might say that I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken when he says that something should be done so that as parliamentarians we can deal intelligently with this subject.
I express regret that the parliamentary and scientific committee which we endeavoured to set up this year when we had before us Professor Bernal, the famed British scientist, has been a great disappointment to me.
I do not agree with the minister to the extent that we should say little about this problem until next year. This is a matter which today is receiving world-wide attention. Surely as one of the nations which are in the know-how we should be doing something more definite about atomic control and. development, and not merely along the lines which we followed during the war, because of necessity at that time we were doing this work as part of our war effort. At this time we should

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
develop atomic energy along peace lines, because I believe there is no single thing which can revolutionize the economies of the world and bring about peace and good will more than atomic energy. At the same time if these fears, which are growing up between the nations today, are allowed to develop, we shall run into difficulties. The minister should do all in his power to cooperate with his colleagues in the government and with those in the international spheres to try to bring about a world development of atomic energy so that this great nuclear power may become a beneficial thing to mankind. We in this country have perhaps one of the main world sources of uranium and plutonium, two of the main ingredients of atomic energy. When we read the reports of these scientists responsible for atomic energy development we are excited by the possibilities of its use for industrial purposes and also for curative purposes in the field of medicine. While keeping atomic energy under government control so that nothing shall be done to curtail its development, we should do everything possible to develop it on an international basis and in such a way as to dispel some of the fears which are abroad today and bring world peace.
What policy is being carried out in regard to the control of the raw material? Are new fields being prospected, and what form of control is exercised?

Any discovery of raw material must be reported to the crown. It cannot be staked privately at the moment. I have stated to the house that I considered that would not be the permanent policy of Canada, but until international negotiations are advanced to a further point the provision against staking by private interests is continued. Eventually, however, I think the control of radioactive materials -will start from the time they are actually mined. They will pass into the hands of the atomic energy control board at that time, and all raw materials from that stage on to the finished product will be handled by the atomic energy control board.

Apparently the minister is not in a position to give us much in the way of details in connection with the development of atomic energy, and the reasons he has given sound fairly reasonable at this time.
I believe, however, he could tell us something about the policy which is being proposed with respect to the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. A moment ago he said something to the effect that it was not the contemplated policy of the government to 
maintain control over the staking of claims or the development of new sources of supply. It was a very hazy statement he made, but I took it to mean that eventually the government proposes to let private enterprise in on the development of atomic energy. It would appear to me that we should have a definite policy very soon, because this is going to be one of the big developments in this country. It can create a new industrial revolution. A new form of power such as that contained in atomic energy can play a major part in the progress of the country, and I fear that if private interests are permitted to come into control of the supply of this material, these same interests, who have other industries in their control using the orthodox forms of energy, will not be inclined to develop atomic energy to its fullest extent. That is only natural because they will want to protect their original investment in the ordinary type of industry. This question therefore poses a problem to parliament. Are we going to do everything possible to see to it that atomic energy is given the fullest opportunity to be developed to its limit for the general use of the country, under public enterprise, or are we going to allow the sources of supply and their development to slip into private hands, as other sources of supply have passed into the hands of private enterprise in the past, with the result that the country is hog-tied and hamstrung by private interests who will not allow their orthodox style of production to be interfered with? It is a matter of history. Although this is not the time to bring out the details, we knowr that private interests in the past have diverted certain processes from production merely because they wished to protect their own investments. That has not been in the interests of the public. Here is one opportunity, surely, for the government to take a step forward for the benefit of the public by developing this form of energjr for the general use of the nation through the initiative of public enterprise. I hope the minister will indicate what the policy of the government is in that connection. Will he tell us whether the government will be prepared to maintain public enterprise in this field and to extend it, or whether they are contemplating handing atomic energy over to private enterprise?

The government is proceeding to develop uses for plutonium. Studies are being made of methods of controlling the release of energy in a manner that will permit it to be used in industry. These studies are in their initial stages, but by the next session of parliament we shall be able to give a report

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
on the advance of the art in that direction. My hon. friend will appreciate that, after this material is produced, methods have to be found for releasing the energy gradually so that it can be used. Theoretically enough of the material could be put in a fountain pen to drive a battleship across the ocean for three years, but the actual mechanics for releasing that energy require a good deal of development. That is work that is being carried on today.

I am not going to press for details. I know that the practical side has to be developed. I would like to know, however, whether the patents of any new invention as a result of atomic energy which is developed by the national research council under the control of the atomic energy control board will be held by the government or by the research council on behalf of the government-
Yes.

-or whether any of them are being disposed of to private interests at this time.
Mr. HOWrE: No.

There is one statement in the report of the atomic energy control board which I do not quite understand. It appears under the heading "Encouragement to Prospecting". It states:
It was not found practicable to make regulations for the encouragement of prospecting, owing largely to uncertainty as to the international situation, but the position is being kept under continuous observation, in cooperation with the Department of Mines and Resources and Eldorado.
That of course is the crown company handling the mines in the northwest territories. Why should it be impossible to encourage prospecting for these necessary minerals? That seems to be of the utmost importance and I do not understand why the board should find it impossible. Furthermore, there is no mention here of cooperation with the provincial departments of mines. They are, at least as far as British Columbia is concerned, and I believe the same is true of Ontario, the bodies which are handling mining. The provincial departments do that. The dominion work in connection with mining is very limited.
It is limited to the northwest territories, but that area contains all the radioactive materials ever discovered.
The people who really know mining are the provincial departments. Will the minister explain that statement I have quoted from the report?

It was explained when the emergency legislation was being discussed. The united nations have not decided whether the control of atomic energy should begin in the ground or not. In the days when Eldorado was formed, control was taken of material in the ground. In other words, the provinces were asked to join with the federal government in enacting legislation to provide that discoveries of radioactive materials should not be patented. That regulation is still in effect. Our inclination was to remove it, but General McNaughton, who represents Canada on the atomic energy commission, felt that any change in the regulations at this time would be unfortunate, that changes should not be made until the policy of the united nations had been determined. Therefore since 1943 no change has been made for that reason.

Does that not mean we are losing precious time in the search for these vital metals? From this report it is quite evident that steps could be taken to encourage prospecting, but those steps are not being taken because we are waiting for the committee of the united nations to reach agreement. If that committee does not make more progress in reaching an agreement in future than it has made in the past we may have to wait quite a long time yet before our board encourages prospecting, and surely Canada should not be losing that time.

The government itself, that is Eldorado, has twenty parties in the field today prospecting for radioactive materials. The Department of Mines and Resources has a few parties also doing the same thing. There is nothing to prevent any prospector from searching for radioactive materials if he wishes. If he makes a discovery, Eldorado will be very glad to take it over and compensate him for it, I do not think there is any great handicap to prospecting. Personally I would prefer that there be no restriction on patenting claims for *radioactive materials, but as I say, the regulations provide otherwise and we have not changed them, following the advice of Genera] McNaughton.
It is perfectly obvious from the report of the board that they believe something should be done to encourage prospecting.
It does not say that.

The report itself is worded in that way: "It was not found practicable to make regulations for the encouragement of prospecting." Obviously the board does know that steps could be taken to encourage prospecting; and I suggest to the minister that this position be given further consideration.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I shall be glad to do that.
The minister has not said anything in regard to cooperation with the provincial departments of mines.
There has been complete cooperation. They have carried out every request this government has made.
Are any of those parties prospecting in the provinces, or are they all in the northwest territories?
In the northwest territories.
So there are no prospecting parties, either under Eldorado or under the dominion Department of Mines and Resources, working in any of the provinces?

I would not say that. I think the Department of Mines and Resources has prospecting parties out in several provinces; but the prospecting parties directly searching for radioactive materials are all in the Northwest territories, if for no other reason than the fact that no discovery of radioactive materials has ever been made outside the Northwest territories.
And is not likely to be unless they start looking.

In
regard to certain discoveries as a result of Which nuclear power could be used for specific industrial purposes I would like to ask the minister how that would be assimilated into Canadian industry. Here we have public research, and let us suppose we find how to use some of this nuclear power in industry. To whom would that privilege be given, and just how would it be assimilated into our Canadian economy? As the hon. member for Dauphin has very well pointed out, there is a problem in that connection when it is realized that such revolutionary uses of nuclear power may upset our economy. I can very well see that the whole progress of atomic research may be retarded unless we have a definite plan to develop it, because you will have the problem of technological unemployment due to bringing such a revolutionary idea as nuclear energy into industry, and you will also have the present system under which that would be a very difficult thing to assimilate. I should like the minister to answer that question.

That is a question that will
not arise for five or six years. There is nothing revolutionary in a government building a source of energy. Governments in this country own more sources of energy than private interests own. The government can either establish a power plant of its own or

sell the rights in the materials to someone else. That is a matter for future governments to determine, however, and I think it would be a waste of time to speculate on it at this moment, when the art is in its infancy.

That is right; the C.C.F.
will determine it.

In any project such
as this, where secrecy is necessary for security reasons, and perhaps particularly in this case, the people are asking questions, and they would like to know the position as far as Canada is concerned. This year we are spending another $5,500,000 on Chalk River. What protection is there to see that the plant, the processes, the research and the results of that research are retained for the good of the Canadian people? Are all the employees at Chalk River government employees, or do you have men there on loan from the United States or other governments, or from firms in other countries? Are there any representatives at that plant from Imperial Chemical Industries or du Pont, and are the details of the processes and research being made available to any persons other than government officials in Canada?

Everyone at Chalk River
is an employee of the government. We do admit visitors from the United Kingdom and the United States, properly sponsored and coming there in the interests of pure science; but only government employees of those two countries sponsored by their governments and coming there for purposes which the government believe are desirable.

In other words all
persons given access to these details of research and so on are sponsored by the governments of other countries?
That is right.

Under section 10 of the Atomic Energy Control Act the board is empowered to set up or incorporate companies. I would like to ask the minister if any companies have been set up or if it is contemplated that any will be set up.

There would be no purpose
in a crown company until the board has a product for sale, which it may have in time. Until that time comes, which will be some time in the future, there would be no purpose in having a crown company and it is not intended to establish any.

I suppose it is quite
improper to ask the minister what is going on at Chalk River, but could he give us any idea of what progress is being made in

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
developing atomic energy materials purely for scientific uses, and what is being done to see that they are not used for war purposes?

All the materials made there are under the control of the government. It is difficult to say more than that. We are making materials, and all the materials are being retained at Chalk River for experimental purposes. That is all I can say.

Item agreed to.
Atomic energy control board

357. Chalk River project-capital and operating expenses, $5,573,000.
Mr. JAQUESr In reference to this atomic energy control board, does that relate to the international control of atomic energy or merely to the control of the development of atomic energy in Canada?
Yes, in Canada.
It has nothing to do with international control?
No.
I do not recall item 356 having been called. Apparently we are calling the odd numbers today; we must have had the even numbers yesterday. Has No. 356 been called?

If it were not so near the end of the session, Mr. Chairman, I might have a good deal to say in reply to that remark. Any discussions I have been carrying on with my associates have been in regard to these items; and if the chairman did not mumble so much we might hear what is going on.

This is a new item dealing with research and investigation with respect to atomic energy. We realize that $150,000 is a mere drop in the bucket when compared with the amount of research taking place. Is this for some special project?

The three universities
indicated have facilities for research ancillary to the work at Chalk River. A cyclotron has been established at McGill university to be used for splitting atoms. At the university of Saskatchewan is a betatron., and at the university of British Columbia a generator and linear accelerator. These have been installed for work in connection with atomic energy, and for that reason these three universities are receiving assistance from the atomic energy control board to let them carry out research which is of value to the work at Chalk River.

In. the last fiscal year the expenditures for Chalk River are shown in the report as amounting to $7,171,067.26, and this year the vote is for $5,573,000. Can the minister give us any idea a.s to how much this project is going to cost each year. Will the expenditure be smaller or will it be increased, and is there any revenue coming in? Is there anything to offset these expenditures?

Not at the present time. The operating cost at Chalk River for the current fiscal year is estimated at $3,400,000. That will be a continuing cost which, in time, we hope will be offset largely by revenue. At the present time however we are not in a position to dispose of any materials which would bring in revenue. So far as capital cost is concerned, the total investment is slightly over $20 million. Provision is made in .the estimate for $5,573,000 which will largely complete the capital expenditure anticipated).
Does this $5,573,000 include operating costs?
The $5,573,000 includes operating costs and capital. The balance of money required is $2,173,000.
And that completes the capital expenditure, on the Chalk River project?
Yes.
Are any of the materials now being produced at Chalk River being exported from Canada, or are they all being held at that point?
They are all being held at Chalk River.
What is that material; is it just a stock pile?
Plutonium, and certain isotropes which are by-products of the process.

568. Departmental administration, $4,989,208.

I take it that the minister or Wartime Housing has not yet arrived at a contract with the city of Vancouver for

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
the building of further houses, and that the minister has not changed bis mind with respect to the Bremerton houses, that he does not propose to bring them in.
This is the vote for departmental administration. Vote No. 574 deals with Wartime Housing Limited.

My remarks will be
general, and will be directed to Wartime Housing Limited, emergency shelter, the moving of buildings, and national housing. I thought this would be the convenient point to discuss all these matters.
As you wish.
I believe I am correct in stating that no agreement has yet been entered into with the city of Vancouver for the building of further houses by Wartime Housing Limited.

No agreement has been
entered into because for months I have found it absolutely impossible to make any agreement with the city of Vancouver. Plans are under way for a very considerable project in that city in the field of low-cost housing. It is not completed, but it has advanced very close to consummation. Certain representatives of the citizens rehabilitation committee are now in the city. They are engaged in developing the project. It is somewhat difficult to discuss the reasons for its not being completed, but I can say we hope to have a thousand low-cost houses under construction there before many weeks go by-but not under agreement with the city of Vancouver.

Having discussed this matter with the minister both privately and in the house on other occasions I should like him to understand that I know his views. I am not accusing him of bad faith in the matter, but I am suggesting that the conclusion to which he has come in respect of wartime housing is wrong.
I believe I am correct when I say that the Bremerton houses are not going to be brought in by the government as emergency shelter, and I should like to deal with that matter for a few moments. I shall be brief, because the minister understands the situation, and it is not necessary to give him details. There are 1,600 houses in Bremerton which could be moved to Vancouver after being obtained from the United States housing authority, the present owner. The estimated landed cost per house on the site and ready for occupation is estimated at 82,100 of which $300 or $400 is reserved for contingencies and allowances for customs duties and items of that kind.
These are four-roomed houses of temporary construction, certainly-not suitable for permanent occupancy-but which come complete, including a certain amount of interior fixtures including such items as stoves and refrigerators. They can be had for somewhere around $2,000-and my best information is that it would be $300 less than that, or $1,700. This project was originated by some, young men in Vancouver. It was pressed by them on the city council and on the minister. They came down here to get in touch with certain insurance companies in the hope of financing the project. The minister was kind to those young men, offering them an emergency shelter grant on each house, and I believe gave them his blessing. In the end however they were unable to get the balance of the funds they needed from the insurance companies.
As I understand it, the reason the minister would not accept these houses as emergency shelter was that they were a little too good to be placed in that class. They had a possible life of about ten years, and did not fall within his specifications as to what emergency shelter should be. The reason why the insurance companies turned down the project-I am not complaining about this because it is their business-was that the houses were not a good commercial risk because their life was limited to ten years. They felt that they could not lend their money on that sort of thing. Therefore, we have these 1,600 houses falling between two stools. On the one hand, it is said they are a little bit too good for us-

I wish my hon. friend would not put words in my mouth. I never said the houses were too good; I always said they were not good enough. I said if anyone wanted to use them for emergency housing we would make a contribution, but I never said they were too good for emergency housing. Nothing could be too good. They might cost too much, but they would not be too good.

I did not intend to suggest that the minister used those words, but the effect of what he said was that $2,000 was too much for one unit of emergency shelter. I am only going by what I understood he said, and he can correct me if I am wrong. The project has failed somewhere between the two methods of getting these houses into Vancouver, between the emergency shelter method and the method of private financing. The one agency would not come up far enough and the other agency would not go down, and the result is that we are not getting these houses.
The housing of veterans who are unable to obtain homes and who have had to double

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
up with their relatives in unsuitable quarters is a social responsibility of this government. The minister recognized that when he said, as reported on page 3595 of Hansard:
The federal government has recognized a responsibility for providing housing to take care of the dislocation in population arising through the war.
Veterans who have had no houses since they came back from overseas are people whose living has been dislocated through the war. The insurance companies very properly say that this social responsibility is up to the government, that it is not up to them. In this unusual situation, which no one would consider except for the housing emergency, they say that they do not intend to take what is called the end position. They say that they have no responsibility for the social end of things. They are quite right in that.
Under all the circumstances of housing in Vancouver I say to the minister that there is a responsibility upon him and upon the government to bring in these houses as emergency shelter, or to provide an adequate number of houses by some other means so that we will not miss the 1,600 houses which could be brought in from Bremerton. Here we have a cut-and-dried project. As he knows he can get most enthusiastic management. The proper person to be in the end position is the government, if there is going to be any end position in this matter. These houses are the cheapest four-roomed houses that can be obtained and they can be obtained most quickly. It may be that the amount of money that w'ould have to be paid for emergency shelter is more than the department has been accustomed to paying, but there is at least a good chance that the money will be got back in the same way that the sponsors of this scheme expected to get it back if they could have raised the money from private sources. I simply want to leave that matter with the minister.
I turn now to wartime housing. In this connection I know the minister feels that the city council has been most uncooperative. I do not hold any brief for the city council. As I understand it, the building of a large number of houses by Wartime Housing in Vancouver this year was prevented by the fact that the city demanded that they be paid an adequate sum for the lots instead of the one dollar which is the usual Wartime Housing payment. The city said that they could not hand them over for one dollar each because their sinking fund would not permit it and they did not want to put the extra cost upon the taxpayers of the city. They held to that position throughout.
On the other hand the government contended that they could not negotiate a different type of contract with Vancouver than had been negotiated with other cities because that would not be fair to the other cities, and they stood on that position. Both sides have stood their ground with the result that the houses have not been built and it looks now as though they will not be built. Vancouver members who have discussed this matter with the minister and the city council have suggested that as the two parties cannot come together, and as the houses are needed, the city and the dominion should agree on terms satisfactory to both and under which the dominion would not pay more than SI for the lot and the city would get what it feels it should get for the lots. As far as I know no progress has been made since that suggestion was offered.
The minister says that he does not want to have one type of contract with one city and another type with, another city. That is all very well, but I find in the Montreal Gazette of Friday, July 4, a report of a scheme similar to the one that Vancouver members proposed which has apparently been entered into between Wartime Housing and Rosemount councillors. One paragraph of this report reads:
The objections of Rosemount councillors have been met by calling for the new houses to be of brick veneer finish, with full basements and pipeless furnaces, although the modifications of the standard Wartime Housing structure will increase rents four to six dollars a month.
That is the suggestion that was made to the minister by the Vancouver members, that he should meet the objections of the Vancouver city council by building the houses and if necessary charging the additional amount to the veterans. By the way, this additional amount as I understand! it would not be more than S2 per month instead of from S4 to S6 per month in the case of the Montreal project. The minister has said that his idea is to keep the rentals of wartime housing, down low, and I agree thoroughly with him in that. I do not think the addition of S2 per month, to the rent of one of these wartime houses in order that the city may get what it feels it should have will raise the rent of any one of these houses over $30 a month, and that is the cheapest rent you can get anywhere. I am sure that a large number of veterans in Vancouver would be prepared to go into that scheme. The minister has broken precedent in Montreal with respect to this matter and I cannot but feel that he could break it for Vancouver just as well. The houses are needed and their building must not be delayed just because two public authorities cannot get together. I am not over-critical of the minister or the city council. I believe

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
that both of them think they are right, but the idea that the inability of two public authorities to agree can stop much needed housing for veterans is one to which I cannot subscribe.
The minister has stated in this house that the dominion has the responsibility for the housing of those dislocated by the war, and no one has been dislocated by the war so much as the veteran.
Why do I feel so strongly on this subject as it relates to the city of Vancouver? The fact is that we have there a very large number of homeless veterans. The February figures, supplied to me by a source in which I have confidence, show that 4,700 veterans were on the waiting list for wartime housing in that month, and of these 2,500 were married men with families with overseas service in the face of the enemy, all of whom had enlisted in Vancouver, so it is in that city where they can most rightfully expect to be housed.
The minister knows that the old Vancouver hotel and the Dunsmuir are sheltering some 400 families and he knows the overcrowding and doubling up that is going on in Vancouver as in other cities.
Just to 'bring it down to an individual basis I have a copy here of the Vancouver Province of Thursday, June 26. which incidentally shows two pictures of a housing survey team looking into housing conditions in Vancouver, and which I shall be glad to show to the minister if he is interested. I want to read some of the things which this survey team found only in June of this year:
One tenement examined by the women was in "imminent danger of collapse," she said. Six families including nine children are living in it.
On the same lot they found three brothers and their mother living in a basement suite "where no daylight could get at them." The brothers are all working and could afford better accommodation, but could find none.
The survey found a veteran and his family living in an alley in a house with all upstairs windows broken and the siding falling off.
Those illustrations give some idea of the conditions with which the minister is very familiar and about which he is much concerned, so I shall not labour that.
The Vancouver Housing Association, which is taking a most active interest in housing in Vancouver, recently informed me that there is a shortage in Vancouver of 25,000 houses. They said if I wanted to be conservative I should say 20,000, so I will say 10,000, and that figure warrants the building of wartime houses at once.
The minister knows that the greatest need of veterans housing is in the lower rental group. So much is that so at the present time in Vancouver that I say again if he does

not bring in Wartime Housing or the Bremerton houses he must do something else, because we cannot go on longer without the housing.
Turning now to a more general approach to the subject, I wish to read two short extracts from newspapers which have caused me considerable alarm. The first is from the Ottawa Citizen of June 24, under the heading: "Home building lagging", and Mr. D. V. Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, is quoted as follows:
He indicated that in the opinion of the government, these figures were lagging sadly from the hoped-for number which Reconstruction Minister Howe included in his 80,000 target for the whole dominion this year.
Referring to the question of materials he said:
"Even if home building were to stop completely," he said, "labour would be fully employed on commercial and industrials construction. so great is the volume of that type of building. The private dwelling situation doesn't look good at all."
The report goes on:
No adequate solution of the complex problem is in sight, he admitted. The only solution lies in getting new homes, and this solution won't be reached for a long time to come.
That simply means that with the stopping of Wartime Housing and the stopping of Housing Enterprises and the stopping of the Veterans Land Act housing scheme, the government is left with only integrated housing as its means of stimulating house building. Integrated housing is a very good scheme., and I think the minister should have ail credit for introducing it, but only a very limited number can take advantage of it. The number of houses that can be built under the integrated housing scheme at the present time apparently is not sufficient to take care of the need.
I have another clipping from the Financial Post of a very recent issue, some time in June. I shall readi only the title of this article:	"Ottawa hopes housing prices to
solve itself. May stand1 by expecting lower cost trend within few months." I do not think this parliament can prorogue without the minister being told that the government should not sit tight and use that way out of this difficulty. In view of the physical need; of housing of so many veterans, that course simply cannot be contemplated. The government must do more than sit tight. It must act, and if it will not act in the way I have suggested in regard to Vancouver, it should ac.t in some other way.
I know it is not my duty to tell the minister how to run his department. It is perhaps sufficient for my simply to point out

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
the shortcomings of the department and leave the minister to find his own way. Nevertheless I shall make one concrete suggestion to him as to how he might help these homeless veterans. The suggestion I am going to make will naturally be a rough one. It might be refined by his officials or by the minister himself; but I would certainly urge it upon him and ask him to take it into consideration. I am going to suggest to him that he do not try any longer to solve the whole housing problem all at once. I am going to suggest to him that he work out a veterans housing scheme, and if he houses the veterans, particularly those who have been homeless since they returned from overseas, he will be doing something for those who are in the greatest need and are the most deserving. At the same time by creating more housing for that class he will loosen up the accommodation for all classes.	.

May I interrupt and say that my hon. friend has evidently not been following the situation closely. Every house that the government has built under wartime housing, under integrated housing, under the Veterans Land Act or under any other government sponsored scheme, has been for veterans and for no one else. The government takes no responsibility for solving the entire housing problem for this country. It is perfectly ridiculous to suggest that it is a government responsibility. Every city has its own housing responsibility, as has every province. The government is responsible for the returned men, and its responsibility stops at that point.
I am perfectly aware that the government has given priority-
Why not say so?

-to veterans under wartime housing, under integrated housing and under all these schemes. I think that is widely enough known, so that the suggestion I am about to make could not have been taken by the minister as a suggestion that he did not give veterans preference in his various schemes. If he would just' listen to me- because I am trying to be helpful-he might find some usefulness in what I say. I am impelled to say it only because of such reports as I see here which suggest that the government is throwing up its hands now and is not going ahead with any of these things.
I am willing to answer my hon. friend, but I am not willing to answer headlines in the Financial Post of Toronto.

I have accomplished
something if I have got a denial of these
headlines from Toronto. Since we see no practical steps being taken and no houses going up under Wartime Housing or under Housing Enterprises Limited or under any government scheme except integrated housing, I think anyone would be pardoned, after looking at the report in the Toronto paper, for being alarmed.
Perhaps the minister will let me go on, because I am really trying to be of assistance to him. If he would rather I simply criticized and sat down I suppose that is all right with me. I should think he would be interested in any scheme which might get him out of his difficulty. If I may go on, I suggest that the minister should work out a scheme to use the veterans, particularly those who have had no accommodation since the end of the war, and there are lots of these. I want to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that even though we have had these schemes under which veterans have had preference, and rightly so, and all credit to the minister for that, there are still many veterans who have not got houses, preference or no preference. There are still many veterans who have had no assistance from the government whatever, no assistance from rent control, because rent control is no good if you have never been in a house. There is a class which has not been reached by any of the minister's schemes for which I am suggesting a veterans housing scheme.
I suggest that in the integrated scheme the minister has the basis for this kind of idea. There is nothing wrong with the integrated scheme except that it is too narrow. There are not enough builders going into it, and they are not building the number of houses which are needed to get roofs over the heads of these veterans. The reason perhaps is that the integrated scheme is what I would call a test tube scheme, a laboratory scheme. It is being tried out in only small units in various places, and it is hedged around by very tight terms and considerations which apparently do not attract builders generally. I suggest to the minister that his veterans housing scheme should be one which utilizes all builders in Canada-the private enterprisers, upon whom he says he relies to get houses built, and the veterans themselves, in order to do the work. I suggest that he expand the integrated scheme; that he prescribe an over-all cost limit and a fairly generous profit limit which will attract more builders into the scheme, and that he use the veterans themselves to make private deals with their own contractor; then if they come to an organization which might be set up with a Legion representative on it, and show that they have a contract for the building of

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
a house within the wider cost and profit limit which I have suggested, that they be given the priority necessary to build the house. In that way the integrated scheme could be expanded widely in every city.
Again we should consider present-day high costs. I suggest to the minister that in all cities we should have had ever since the end of the war a veterans housing scheme following the principle of the Veterans Land Act small holdings scheme. He might now consider all those veterans who have never had houses but who now still have reestablishment credits. I understand that only one-third of the reestablishment credits have been used. I suggest that he enable them to finance themselves in these times of high cost, if they will give up their reestablishment credit, by giving them benefits of the same kind as under the small holdings scheme under the Veterans Land Act. In that way he may be able to provide financing for many veterans who would like to build but have not the money.
The minister knows of the Canadian Legion suggestion that he should lend up to ninety per cent of cost instead of ninety per cent of lending value with the same over-all cost and profit restriction. The minister might well investigate that in this type of scheme.
I now want to turn to the question of providing rental housing. When the minister made his-

If I may reply, the hon. member has been labouring a scheme that has been in operation for years. Any veteran who has $600 can build a house under provisions passed by this parliament which provide that a veteran may borrow ninety-five per cent of the first $3,000 and eighty-five per cent of the second $3,000, which means ninety per cent of the loan on a house with a lending value of $6,000, and somewhat more for a house costing less. He can arrange with the contractor to build it under the integrated scheme or he can arrange with the contractor to build it privately. On a total investment of $600 he can build a $6,000 house anywhere he likes.

The minister knows better than I that the number of contractors who are taking part in the integrated plan is very small compared to the number of contractors in Canada. There is something about that scheme which is not widely attracting the builders of the country. I suggest to the minister that it may be due to the fact that the scheme is a little too rigid andi so is not having the practical result which one might expect from the theory underlying it. After all, I would not be here talking at all if the housing conditions in Canada, and particularly in Vancouver, were not as I have described

them, and the result of all these good 'theories of the minister has not been to put these men in homes.
It has built a lot of houses, though, hasn't it?
I am afraid I did not hear what the minister said.
I't has built a good many houses.

I want to give the minister all credit, because I know thait this is a difficult- problem, but he cannot ask me to admit that it has resulted in the building of ' a good many houses. The minister has given us the figures himself.
There were 175,000 since the war ended.

There were 6,800 wartime houses and 6,141 units of emergency shelter completed last year; and of course there were 3,000 integrated or less than 3,000, which is about 15,000 out of 60,000 completed by all means.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

Let us not talk nonsense. This government sponsored a programme for post-war building of houses which produced about 53,000 in 1945, 62,000 in 1946 and, it is hoped, will produce 80,000 in 1947. Let us not have any juggling of the figures. That is close to 200,000 houses.

The minister's own
senior officer has publicly pointed out the danger that we shall not reach 80.000. I do not want to get into an argument with the minister over the comparative number of houses built. I am thinking of the fact that two years after the war a very large number of veterans, who should have the highest priority in the country, have no houses, despite all schemes. I do not think it profits us to talk about 60,000 or 80.000 or 200,000.
I am talking about 4,700 in Vancouver who want houses now, after all these things have been done.
It may be that what I have suggested is very like the minister's integrated scheme; indeed, I said it was. I said it was only an expansion of that scheme. I am suggesting to the minister that he should expand it.
Now I wish to speak for a moment about the rental side of the problem. In February of this year the minister, as reported at page 211 of Hansard, speaking of that problem, stated in part:
Because rental construction was disappointingly low in 1946, we believe that steps should be taken to remedy this deficiency.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
Then he set out certain steps which he proposed to take, such as double depreciation, a longer term of amortization and priorities for those who built rental housing. I do not think the minister's scheme has produced much more rental construction. He can correct me if I am wrong in that,, but I do not think it has had the effect which he desired, and which I believe the house hoped for as much as he did, At page 212 of Hansard of the same day he said:	*
We believe that these steps will substantially increase the supply of new rental housing units. Should' we be wrong, other steps must be taken, because we cannot allow a continuation of the proportionately low level of new construction in this field.
He was speaking of the rental field. I know that the minister considers it not to be his duty to subsidize rental housing. He said so quite clearly. I suggest to him, however, that so far as veterans are concerned we have a special problem. It might very well be singled out from the general situation in regard to low rent housing. In these particularly difficult times, right after the war, I submit that he should give special consideration to that particular class no matter what his general views may be.
The minister knows that in this low monthly rental field the houses are not going up. I suggest to him that he make use of the same technique as he adopted in the war when he needed ships. He built the ships, retained ownership in the crown, and operated them through private ship operators. When the war was over and the need for these ships for war purposes had disappeared, he was able to sell the ships to private operators at a price which, in his opinion and in the opinion of these operators, would enable them to keep the ships at sea in peace-time trade and so make possible the maintenance of the merchant marine. I do not see why that same idea could not be followed in the matter of veterans rental housing. If as a resuLt of that plan the government suffered loss, that loss could be capitalized and considered as a war expenditure, precisely in the same way as with wartime ship building.
I see it is one o'clock and therefore I will say nothing further now. I assure the minister, however, that while I am most critical of him I am critical not for what he has done but for the results which he has failed to achieve- everything that I have said has been said in a sincere desire to help him in what is Canada's major problem.
Progress reported.
