speechtext:
Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue and Minister of National War Services) moved the second reading of Bill No. 453, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936.
He said: Mr. Speaker, since the passing of the Canadian Broadcasting Act in 1936 and the setting up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the affairs of the corporation, including its policies, its operation and its financial statement have been under review by a special committee in successive years. That custom was followed this year, so I submit that anyone who is interested in the affairs of the corporation or in radio broadcasting has had a splendid opportunity to follow the debates that have taken place. Having followed them, such person must be informed with reference to the matters which have been under discussion. Therefore I do not feel that I should take much time today in any attempt to review the situation in reference to the broadcasting corporation. This bill is an amendment to the Canadian Broadcasting Act. It is not a very long measure, and has to do principally with the amendment of one section.
Under the Canadian Broadcasting Act the proceeds of radio licence fees go to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At present costs of administration and collection are deducted. The special committee on radio broadcasting last year recommended that the full amount of the fees paid go to the C.B.C. The broadcasting committee this session has reiterated this recommendation. In a report presented to the house last Friday, the committee said:
Your committee has reviewed the financial position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation very carefully this year and is impressed with the need of the corporation for a larger income, and the committee believes that the whole of the licence fee received from holders of receiving sets should be paid over to the corporation by the Department of Transport. A like report was made last year and your committee regrets that same was not implemented. Your committee recommends that appropriate legislation be passed at this session to give effect to this recommendation.
I submit that the committee had a good opportunity to consider the financial aspects of a national radio system after hearing full explanations from officials of the C.B.C.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

It is seldom realized how great are the basic costs of operating a national radio system in Canada. The operation of a nationwide system in this country is basically more expensive per head than it is in any other country that has a nationwide system. This is due to the fact first of all that Canada has a very big area with a relatively small population. No matter how it is done it costs money to cover a given, area with a radio programme; thus costs per head in Canada of getting programmes to listeners are very high. For example, one single station in New York can cover a population as great as that of all Canada. To reach the same number of people in this country we need thirty or more stations and thousands of miles of expensive wire lines in regular daily operation. Thus the basic cost per head of reaching listeners is many times greater in Canada than in the United States.
The area of Great Britain is only a fraction of the area of the inhabited part of Canada. But to provide services, the British Broadcasting Corporation has the revenue from the £1 licence fee of over ten million people. On its home services this year the B.B.C. has over S40,000,000 to spend. The C.B.C., with its vast and expensive area to cover, had some §5,800,000 from all sources. In Australia the licence fee is also £1. In New Zealand the rate is 25 shillings, and in South Africa an average of 28 shillings. Neither Great Britain nor Australia faces the need of providing broadcasting service in two languages. In Canada this increases our basic cost by a very considerable proportion. It means duplicate facilities in part of the country, extra administration costs, and large extra programme costs.
In the face of the high cost factors set by the nature of Canada and the composition of our nation, the C.B.C. has been operating a national radio system with a licence fee of §2.50 compared with higher fees in other countries. Actually it has been receiving only about an average of §2.15 per licence. The national system also receives some assistance in programming and some additional revenue from commercial sources. But the financial basis of a national radio system in Canada is, and probably will continue to be, direct contributions from the public. Comparisons with other radio systems show that the revenues of the C.B.C. are small in relation to the size of the job it has to do in Canada. During recent years its expenditures have necessarily increased to meet needs of the listening public. Broadcasting facilities and network service have extended to cover wider areas. This involves extra operating costs which continue year by year.

At the same time the corporation has been faced by sharply rising costs in nearly every phase of its activities. In the last few years prices and costs in almost every field have gone up in Canada. In the radio business this rise has been particularly acute. For example, a comparison between the performers' fee costs of a group of typical programmes in 1940 and for the same programmes at today's rates shows an increase of sixty per cent. Expenditure items of the C.B.C. have risen ; at the same time the main income item of the licence fee has remained at the same level. No organization can remain in the situation where costs rise steeply while its income remains about the same, and still continue to give good service.
For the year 1945-46 the corporation had an operating deficit of §78,000. Last year costs again increased considerably, but by careful management and economies, which had to include a reduction in employment given to Canadian artists, the corporation succeeded in keeping its operating deficit at S70,000. In this it was assisted by a rise in commercial revenues and in the total number of licence fees paid. No great help, however, can be expected from these sources in the future. The number of families owning radio sets cannot grow much larger than it is today unless we have within a short time a considerable increase in population. Efforts by the corporation to increase its commercial revenues too greatly would seriously reduce the quality of the service given by the national system.
Deficits of the corporation are met out of its own limited reserves saved from surpluses in earlier years. I might point out here that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been financed entirely by the people of Canada through moneys they have paid in licence fees, and fees by commercial revenue. It is true that loans have been made to the corporation. In every instance those loans have been repaid. The corporation had power to borrow, and at the present time has a loan for increased capital expenditure. In due course we hope that that loan too will be paid. When I say that every loan has been paid, I mean that that is the condition up to last year.
On the basis of its present operations, the corporation would face a deficit of at least §265.000 this year. Therefore if the proposed extra revenue were not provided, the corporation would have drastically to reduce more of its services and its use of Canadian artists and writers.
Giving the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the full amount of licence fees paid will provide extra revenue to meet at least some of

Canadian Broadcasting Act
the increases in its costs. If this were not done it would mean inevitably serious deterioration in the extent and quality of the service provided by the national system. It would mean that the corporation could not maintain present broadcasting produced by Canadians for Canadians. It would certainly mean that necessary improvements could not be made.
I think that this house agrees that our national broadcasting system is providing an important and valuable service for the Canadian people from coast to coast. It is one means of bringing together Canadians in whatever part of the country they live, and it makes an important contribution to our national life.
This bill, carrying out the recommendations of two parliamentary committees, will enable the national radio system, to continue its present service to the Canadian public.
Mr. DONALD M. speechtext:
I was referring to the fact that in the many years since 1935 that the committee on radio broadcasting has sat, there has never been a motion for concurrence in a report. It is only therefore on an occasion of this kind, when a bill is presented, that one is afforded an opportunity to discuss this important question of radio broadcasting in Canada.
We are frequently reminded in the radio committee and in the house by spokesmen for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that their responsibility is to parliament. If the responsibility is to parliament, and that is the statutory position, then certainly it is desirable that the reports from the committee from year to year should be debated in the house on motions for concurrence, if for no other purpose than to let the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation know whether the recommendations in the reports presented from year to year really represent the view of parliament.
If a motion for concurrence were made in the house it would serve as a guide to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. If there
Canadian Broadcasting Act

is to be true parliamentary control of that corporation, then obviously there should be some vehicle provided for an effective expression of views, not only in this one house of parliament, but in both houses. This is particularly true because, in the light of the experience I have had on that committee in the past two sessions of parliament, I can say it has been dominated by a working majority of Liberal and C.C.F. members who are, at least in this instance, apparently on completely common ground.
Another important reason in my estimation why the reports of this committee should be fully debated in the house is that it would afford an opportunity to see whether the expressions of the Liberal-C.C.F. majority in the committee actually represented the views of this House of Commons. In the closing stages of the session last year, during the debate on a bill which was similar to the one now before the house but included other matters a? well, an opportunity was afforded, as now, to discuss the report of the committee. I would remind lion, members that the discussion which followed then had a different flavour and tone from that which prevailed in the committee.
As the minister pointed out when introducing the bill, in effect the house is being asked to approve a proposal that the consolidated revenue fund of Canada should bear the entire cost of collecting fees imposed on private stations and owners of receiving sets. On the basis of last year's figures the amount involved is $544,673.17 per annum. To a government dominated by the mental approach indicated by one senior member of the cabinet who said in the house in 1945 when speaking on his estimates, "what's a million dollars?" this amount probably does not look like a large sum. However, on further examination I think the house will see that there is more involved in this matter than simply the question of giving the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a sum annually in excess of half a million dollars.
Just in passing I should like to mention several factors bearing on this present proposal. First, the amount is annual and it may increase. The minister thinks that there will not. be any substantial increase in the number of licensees of receiving sets. He may be right,, but I am inclined to think that there is going to be an increase; therefore the cost of administration and collection is likely to rise. This bill proposes that the cost of administration and collection shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund, which
[Mr. Fleming.)
would give the C.B.C. the gross rather than merely the net revenue from these fees.
These costs of administration and collection are too high. In the past eight years they have never been less than 11-92 per cent of the total fees collected. They have risen to as high as 12-5 per cent and last year they were 12-36 per cent of the total. That is much too high. In addition, the enforcement apparently is not the same in all parts of the country. As was admitted by one minister last Tuesday, apparently the enforcement is much more strict in Ontario than it is in other provinces.
There is a much more serious aspect, to this matter. The public wants to know what it costs to maintain the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It has known that hitherto because every licencee of a private receiving set has had- an annual reminder of that cost- every time he paid his licence fee. He knew what he had to pay for the benefits of the enterprises of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. He will continue to pay $2.50 per year, but that $2.50 will no longer represent the total cost of maintaining the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There will be provided by parliament from the consolidated revenue fundi-I take it that it will be done by a statutory item-a sum in excess of half a million dollars per annum. I do not till ink that, is sound in principle. I do not think additional revenue should be provided and then the impression left with the people-I do not think it is intentional, but it is inevitable-that the $2.50 is providing everything necessary to maintain the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I know why the government does not propose to increase the licence fees by an amount sufficient to provide what is 'being provided by this bill. The minister has indicated that the additional payment to C.B.C. will equal 35 cents for each receiving set licence. Why does not the government increase the receiving licence fee to $2.85 or $3.00? I will tell you why. It would be a most unpopular move; there would be an outcry across the country. Yet this bill is indirectly increasing it. It may not be intentional, but this method has the effect of hiding part of the cost of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation from the public. It is an unsound method. The cost should not be hidden in this way.
What is this additional money going to be used for? After all, that is the crux of the whole matter. The minister has indicated that the costs of operation are rising. That is quite true. He has referred also to deficits. These are manifest from the evidenoe heard

Canadian Broadcasting Act
by the committee. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946, the C.B.C. statement showed an operating deficit, before providing allowances for depreciation and obsolescence, of $78,425.73. An officially audited statement for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947, is lot yet available but the estimate of the officials of the C.B.C. is that the operating deficit, without including allowances for depreciation and obsolescence, will aggregate about $70,000, approximately the same as last year. The minister stated this afternoon that there is an actual operating deficit for the year 1945-46 of $265,000, and we had a repetition of that last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: No. I said the anticipated deficit for this year, 1947-48, was $265,000.

The figures are practically the same on the basis of actual operating deficit without allowances for depreciation and obsolescence, and I do not think there is any reason to expect that there would be any great difference between the two years in the actual deficit including proper allowances for depreciation and obsolescence.
For what purpose is this additional money being provided? Is it simply a matter of improving the service to the Canadian people? That depends upon what you mean by service. In my submission this additional amount is not chiefly for the improvement of programmes and for the employment of more Canadian talent, a worthy and laudable object. It is tied in with a policy of expansion by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is the same policy which was discussed during the debate in the closing stages of the session last year.
This policy of expansion does not confine itself to the occupation by the C.B.C. of channels not hitherto occupied. It is a policy of expansion which takes on a most aggravated form in the assumption by this corporation of three of the major wavelengths now in the hands of private stations, stations which represent in terms of actual operation the closest thing we have in Canada today to competition in radio as between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and others. Parliament must ask itself at this juncture whether it approves this policy of expansion.
It is not enough to say that parliament last year in the closing stages of the session provided in a supplementary appropriation another loan of $2,000,000 for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that there was presented to this house a bill which among other things provided that there should be opened up to C.B.C. loans aggregating $10,000,000 over a 83166-3521
period, and in the first fiscal year $2,000,000 of that sum was to be available by way of loan to C.B.C. The whole basis of it was to enable the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to embark on an extensive policy of expansion, expansion in the form of providing an additional network. It was not simply a matter of improving the programmes of one national network. This programme of expansion contemplated the creation of a second national network, namely, the dominion network and the taking over of CFCN as part of the trans-Canada network; the dominion network was to take over the wave length of CFRB and transfer it to CJBC and make that the foundation for the second dominion network. Parliament did not pass that bill. It never was given second reading, and I submit that in passing the supplementary appropriation this house did not give approval to a programme of expansion in the form of a second national network as proposed in the bill. I submit that parliament has a duty at this stage to review this whole question of expansion, expansion at the expense of the wave lengths now enjoyed by some privately-owned stations which are among the leaders in giving service to the public.
Since that time the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has proceeded with very fcreat haste in its steps to take over these wave lengths and crowd these three stations out into inferior wave lengths because the equal of the three they have enjoyed are now no longer available. They were available some years ago if C.B.C. had made know its intentions then, but it did not. The time limit provided by international agreement on this' continent for the increase of power on class 1-A channels to 50,000 watts, has been' extended by a modus vivendi arrangement. Nevertheless C.B.C. is proceeding with all' possible speed to take over and occupy these wave lengths. That was done with government concurrence. It had to be. The government did approve. It had to approve before these three stations could be displaced from wave lengths which they had occupied for some years and on which they had given the Canadian listening public very good service.
Therefore I submit to this house that this whole question resolves itself now into this. Is the house prepared to give blanket approval to a policy of expansion which has as its foundation the taking over of these wave lengths held by the privately-owned stations? The report of the radio committee says:
The area of competition between C.B.C. and the privately-owned stations is small.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

That is the expression in the report, in the Votes and Proceedings, at page 737. The area of competition is small. The report says elsewhere:
The functions of the two types of radio service are different.
-that is, C.B.C. on the one hand and the privately-owned stations on the other, and there are about 100 of these stations in Canada. The report also says that these two types of radio service should be complementary to one another. In that respect I submit that the finding of the radio committee is not a correct and factual finding. Actually there is a very considerable area of competition as between C.B.C. on the one hand and the privately-owned stations on the other. That is the whole basis of the complaint which the privately-owned stations have made, through their association, against the continuation of a system under which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not only competitor, not only litigant, but also judge and policeman over them. If the situation were as simple as the radio commission has so naively described it, and there were no element of competition between the C.B.C. on the one hand and the privately-owned station on the other, the case for an independent regulatory tribunal would be somewhat different. But there is no escape from the fact that there is a substantial element of competition between the C.B.C. on ithe one hand and the privately-owned stations on the other.
The chairman of the board of C.B.C. said at a recent meeting that the evidence he would be prepared to give this year would be confirmatory of the evidence he gave to last year's committee on the matter of competition. To last year's committee he said that 'the C.B.C. *was in competition with the privately-owned stations for listener interest-that	was
admitted-and in competition with them for jommercial revenue. Those are important indicia of competition. I well remember putting a question to the chairman of the board of C.B.C. I want to make clear that the chairman of the board of C.B.C. is a gentleman for whom I have the highest respect. He is very efficient, and I think is gifted with ,a high sense of public service. He agreed that the place where competition wras the keenest was where C.B.C. comes into competition with the large privately-owned stations of the kind I have referred to, the kind which enjoy the three wave lengths which are being taken over by C.B.C. with the government's full approval in what is nothing else tout what I would call legalized robbery.
Here is the position. There is an area of *competition. The C.B.C. was given by the
[Mr. Fleming.!
Broadcasting Act the widest kind of powers to regulate all broadcasting in Canada. It is very difficult to conceive of powers couched in wider language than those contained in sections 8 and 22 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act. It gives C.B.C. control of all the private stations. It is a most sweeping power. Not only that, but the full licensing authority for all radio stations in Canada is vested by the Radio Act in the Minister of Transport, whose functions-which we were considering the other night-are exercised by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply'. He acts in pursuance of section 24 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act on the recommendation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It was stated in evidence that he has never gone counter to the recommendations of C.B.C. in this matter. To all intents and purposes with the approval of the government the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation not only has full and complete regulatory powers in respect of all radio broadcasting in Canada but it shares with the Minister of Transport complete authority in respect of the issuing of licences.
In that situation I submit that the only fair and proper way in which parliament ought to make provision for legislative control over broadcasting in Canada, including licensing, is by vesting authority in the public interest in an independent regulatory tribunal. Independent-why do I say that? It must be independent of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have said already that that body, even in the area in which it is in close competition with private stations, is their judge. They have no right to appeal from its judgment. It is the one and final judge. Is that not a fine situation? Here is one competitor coming before its chief competitor as a litigant, and the latter competitor has not only his interests involved as a litigant but he is judge, jury and sheriff, and in the case of these three wave lengths, executioner as well. I submit that that is an absolutely unhealthy situation. It is very unhealthy for the C.B.C.
I must confess my difficulty in understanding the attitude taken by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, voiced in the committee recently by the chairman of the board. I think with the full approval of the board of governors, that when the Canadian Association of Broadcasters comes before the parliamentary committee and asks that an independent regulatory tribunal be set up in the public interest it flies to arms and says: We are being attacked. I do not approve of that attitude. I do not think that because the C.B.C. is given these functions it. should regard itself as

Canadian Broadcasting Act
inviolate, or that it should be regarded as an act of impertinence on the part of those with whom it is in competition, in a substantial area of competition, to come to the only place that they can come and say they think the system is wrong and it ought to be changed. Surely we have not yet come to the place in this country where persons who have a grievance cannot come to a parliamentary committee and pleadi for a change in. the system under which they are being judged by their competitors.
When we are told that these people did not set forth individual complaints. I ask, Mr. Speaker, if we need any more individual complaints than the record of the legalized robbery by the C.B.C. of these three wave lengths. For my part I do not need any more proof of the necessity of some tribunal standing apart from the C.B.C. to judge as between the C.B.C. and the private stations in these matters where their interests are in headlong conflict. The kind of tribunal that is needed, Mr. Speaker, is a tribunal which, in the field of regulation of broadcasting in Canada and with respect to licensing of stations for the purpose of broadcasting in Canada, would exercise powers and functions similar to those exercised in the field of transportation in Canada by the board of transport commissioners. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, parliament countenancing a proposal that the functions of the board of transport commissioners in respect of the regulation of rail transport in Canada should be handed over to the Canadian National Railways? Would you think of submitting the Canadian Pacific Railway to regulation by its competitor the Canadian National Railways? It is not enough to say that in the railway field the competition is complete, and that in the broadcasting field the competition is not so complete. That is an answer in degree only, and apparently we differ very greatly on the extent of the degree. For my part I say that the principle involved is precisely the same.
I will give another example. The air transport board, in a manner somewhat similar to the board of transport commissioners in its field, regulates civil aviation in Canada. It has had to judge as between Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and will no doubt have to do it on occasions in the future. Would this house countenance a proposal that these regulatory functions in respect of civil aviation in Canada should be handed over to Trans-Canada Air Lines to be judge over its competitor? Of course no sensible hon. member would propose any such thing. Then why in the field of radio broadcasting do we-in the face of the case that has been made out for an independent regulatory tribunal appointed with full parliamentary approval, holding tenure, possessing powers, exercising functions, and generally operating in the same fashion in its field as the board of transport commissioners in the railway field-why do we hesitate now to take action to correct the situation that is now permitted to exist here? I say, Mr. Speaker, the time has come when this house must boldly say that we believe in public control of all radio broadcasting, and that we are going to say that, as between the various agencies through which broadcasting is done in Canada, there will be fair play. The Only way in which that can be assured is through an- independent tribunal appointed under parliamentary authority and operating in the public interest.
I want to deal as quickly as I can with several individual matters. Reference will be found in the report of the radio committee to the matter of a ceiling. The ceiling on the strength of private stations in Canada is set by C.B.C., and as things now stand no private station has any chance of being allowed to increase its power to the point where C.B.C. is likely to experience too much competition from that station. There are only a couple of stations, being those holding these wave lengths to which I have referred, which enjoy any power in advance of the ceiling set by the C.B.C. for all privately owned stations in Canada, which is 5.000 watts. The result is that, depending on which of two alternative interpretations of the Havana treaty, section 6, is correct, we may have been losing some of the prior rights we had in respect of channels which were assigned to us from the class 2 channels under that treaty.
The radio committee has brought forward a proposal now which is sensible though belated, indicating that it does think the ceiling may well be raised. I submit that should have been done long ago. It would have been in the public interest. Greater power for these stations would mean better broadcasting. better reception at the receiving end, and generally better service to the Canadian people. The final decision on this question of ceiling should not be left in the hands of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Then there is the matter of television and facsimile. Facsimile is not mentioned in the report, although we heard much evidence on it. There should have been something in the report on facsimile. Nobody may have a licence unless the C.E C. board recommends it. The C.B.C. has refused heretofore to
Canadian Broadcasting Act

recommend the issuance of any licence for television and facsimile. Why? The reason is the paternalistic attitude taken by the C.B.C. They say that this country is not ready for facsimile and television; that it would be premature for somebody to spend money on it. They think it is premature for the C3.C. *to spend money on it, but they will not let private interests spend their own money to develop facsimile and television. Can you imagine a situation like that, Mr. Speaker? I call that the final proof of the dangers of the monopolistic control over radio broadcasting by C.B.C. What we are going to wake up one day in this country and find is that television in the United States is an established fact and in commercial use. In Canada C.B.C. will then begin to consider whether it should permit anybody to have such a licence.
This report-again it is a belated recommendation; again in strict fact it is a censure of the policy followed by the government and the broadcasting corporation-recommends that consideration be given to the granting of licences for television, provided*-and this is a proper proviso-the licencee will really develop, these licences and spend money and work on the development of television. That is sensible. Nobody should have a licence simply to be allowed to sit on his rights; but there are people who have been applying for these licences and have indicated they are prepared to spend money on them. But the almighty C.B.C.. with the almighty minister who is the fountain of licences says: No; we are going to exercise paternalistic control over you and we are not going to allow you to have a licence. We are not going to let you spend your money to develop television in Canada.
The same thing applies to facsimile. The possibilities of the development of facsimile in Canada as elsewhere are simply revolutionary, Mr. Speaker, and if we are just going to sit by we are leaving the newspapers of this country exposed to the danger,-I do not say the certainty-of being found at a great disadvantage when facsimile becomes a proven fact. If the C.B.C. then exercises the ruling powers that it enjoys under section 8 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act to publish news, the newspapers may he completely at the mercy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I wish to deal with one further matter in the report. There is a criticism in this report which represents the views of the Liberal-C.C.F. alliance on the committee. I think an attempt is made in several paragraphs to smear the private stations. When we are
[Mr. Fleming. 1
told that they are making a lot of money, I would remind the house that these stations were not given any opportunity to indicate, nor were they asked any questions about, their profits. We simply find quoted verbatim in the report a statement given by C.B.C. We are not told what that represents in terms of the past operating records of these stations. We are not told anything about their experience in the pioneer days. These stations were not given an opportunity to be heard on this point, but an attempt is made here to smear them.
The private stations are also criticized inferentially in this report for even daring to publicize, over their own stations and in the press, the brief which they were submitting to the committee. Think of that! Apparently we have come to the pass in this parliament where a committee, dominated by the government-C.C.F. alliance, can criticize people because they try to make their views known across Canada even though they are expressing those views at the same time before a parliamentary committee. That is one faint example of the dangers that exist today in our radio set-up of throttling and muzzling free expression of public opinion in Canada.
When this report undertakes to criticize the privately-owned stations for not using more live Canadian talent, I would make this observation. I for one want to make it perfectly clear that in my opinion the private stations and the C.B.C. alike are not using enough live Canadian talent, and if the private stations are not doing so, it is an indictment of the C.B.C. for its failure to exercise wisely its regulatory powers over those stations. I do not think enough has been done to encourage the greater use of Canadian live talent over these stations, and I will tell you one reason for that. It is the insecurity of tenure enjoyed by the private stations. They have a licence which is clearly stated to be for twelve months only; it expires on March 31 of each year. They have therefore no legal assurance of continuance beyond that date. This committee has wisely reported in favour of some extension of that tenure, because if these stations are given some assurance of tenure, encouragement will be given them to expend more of their revenues in the development and use of Canadian talenf.
I believe this report is right in its recommendation that the present refusal of the C.B.C. to grant licences to newspapers ought to be withdrawn. There is no reason why newspapers as such should not be permitted to hold radio licences pending good behaviour

Canadian Broadcasting Act
like any other licensee. The fact is that a number of newspapers have licences, and if you deny the same right to other newspapers you are putting those that now possess licences in a favoured position, and that is indefensible discrimination.
The same thing applies to multiple ownership. I say that, other things being equal, we should try to spread licences around. Where other things are absolutely equal, where you have competing applications, the licence should be granted to the applicant who has not already a licence, but there should be no rule against the ownership of more than one station. That is arbitrary and it favours those who already enjoy the ownership of more than one station. Again, that is indefensible discrimination.
There are omissions from this report'. It is clear, from what I have said, what kind of omissions they are.
I wish to conclude these remarks by pointing out the dangers of the present situation. Anyone who will sit down and calmly examine the possibility that exists, through the monopoly of licensing, not necessarily under the present management but under any other management, of throttling the free expression of public opinion, will realize that these dangers are so great that the time has come when this house must see that the structure of radio broadcasting in Canada is recast, that the regulating and licensing are confided to a body publicly appointed, operating in the public interest, which will function with due regard for the interests of all, instead of being dominated by the C.B.C. We must avoid monopoly and make a more realistic approach to the whole problem, and I say that if the house passes this bill, having regard to what we know now about the plans of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for expansion, we are extending powers which it is too dangerous in this or any other country, to confide, to one agency.

We have listened once again to the annual hymn of hate of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), and it was not quite so good as it was last year, perhaps because there was so much duplication of material in it. I would suggest to the Tory party that they get another needle or another record, or at least that they get some live talent on their programmes. I think they could do with it. The member for Eglinton has talked repeatedly of the C.C.F.-Liberal majority. I can assure him that Canada under these circumstances is much better off with a C.C.F.-Liberal majority than under the rather insanitary Tory-Social Credit minority.
One of the things I have noticed about the member for Eglinton is his habit of saying nothing with an air of great profundity. For instance, he tells us that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the judge, jury, sheriff and executioner as well, and he tells us that is not a healthy situation. I have never known execution to be at all healthy, but that is a matter which, the hon. member for Eglinton can decide for himself. However, if he is guilty of these profundities he is equally guilty of enunciating error with a zeal worthy of a better cause. For instance, he asks us this question:	Is the house prepared to give
approval to this policy of taking over channels owned by private radio? There are no channels owned by private radio. They belong to the people of Canada and the people have complete control at any time over these channels.
In another burst of oratorical fervour he asks us to watch that freedom of expression is not throttled and muzzled by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Canada. It is possible I have had more radio experience than my hon. friend. During the last twelve years I have made as many as 800 or 900 broadcasts on the C.B.C. and private stations, and my practical experience is that liberty is in no danger whatsoever from the C.B.C. But liberty would be in danger if the C.A.B.-the Canadian Association of Broadcasters-were running things in this country.
What is asked for in this bill is in effect that another half million dollars of revenue be given the C.B.C. The corporation needs it. It has had a deficit, and if it cannot get more revenue there is only one thing to be done and that is to cut certain sustaining programmes. If the C.B.C. gets its revenue, not only will it be able to maintain its service to the people of Canada but it will be able to improve that service. The alternative is to cut certain programmes and they will be sustaining programmes, the type of programmes that appeal to a minority in the country, but a minority which must not be lost sight of.
There is "Stage 47." On occasion I have heard some bad performances, but on the whole I think the presentations "Stage 47" and "Stage 46" and those of previous years have been a credit to radio in Canada, and I should toe sorry to. see them dispensed with. We have the weekly book reviews, the forums, chamber concerts and so on, and all these things must be paid for. A substantial minority of people in Canada want to hear these things, as I have said, and if the C.B.C. cannot get the revenue we just will not hear them. We have symphony concerts from Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, and I hope that next year we may have such con-
Canadian Broadcasting Act

certs from Winnipeg. Unless the C.B.C. steps in, however, there will be no orchestra at all in Winnipeg. As a matter of fact there are very few symphony orchestras which do not require to be subsidized in some way. I remember that in 1938 three of us in that western city were talking about. . the possibility of building a symphony orchestra in Winnipeg. One of the three was the western director for the C.B.C., Mr. Claringbull; another was Mr. Geoffrey Waddington, the well known musician and conductor, and I was the third!. Through the cooperation and help given by the C.B.C. eventually we were able to build up in Winnipeg an orchestra of some fifty-five men and women, who became sufficiently good as performers to be heard not only over the Canadian network but also over the Mutual network in the United States. That would have been impossible without the aid of the C.B.C. I think the orchestra got about $400 a programme, and even at that it meant the players averaged over a period of ten weeks only about $10 per performance, which is inadequate pay for the performances they gave.
So if the C.B.C. is going to avoid running into deficits, some of the most- cultural and useful programmes in Canada will have to be dispensed with. The minister has told us that much of the service given by the C.B.C. is provided by the licence fee of $2.50 paid by the citizens of Canada. He has also told us that we are reaching the saturation point-in the number of licences that can be issued. The rise in fee revenue apparently has been checked in the last three years; but while that has become stationary every other phase of cost has climbed steeply. There is administrative, operational and programme cost; and, as the minister said, the fees of artists have increased by almost sixty per cent in some cases since 1940. Unfortunately the salaries of those who work for the C.B.C. have not risen in proportion to the cost of living. It is not right that these public servants s-hould be discriminated against because sufficient revenue is not available for them, -because the inevitable result will be the loss, not only to the corporation but to Canada, of many of our most able young men and women.
I do not think there can be any question that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the greatest instrument we have in Canada for the advancement of culture. I do not suggest that there is yet any such thing as a Canadian culture. We are still falling between the two influences, the British and the American, and it is time we started to build our own. In this the Canadian Broadcasting {Mr. Stewart.]
Corporation can be of great assistance. The type of culture we are importing from south of the line just now unfortunately is mainly that of the comic strip. Without wishing to give offence I think I can suggest that Li'l Abner is much better known than most cabinet ministers, and in certain cases perhaps held in higher esteem. It is obvious that if we are going to produce a Canadian culture we must be prepared to pay for it, and one of the tasks of the C.B.C. is to develop and expand this particular form of service to all the people of Canada. That, is a policy of expansion; and the C.B.C. should be continually expanding if the type of service we envisage is to be given. We have to give coverage to the most sparsely populated areas in our country, and that is expensive. It means that in Canada the cost per head for coverage is probably higher than in any other country. We have a great area with a small population; therefore it is obviously expensive to provide the service we expect our people to get. I stress that word "service" because it is the duty of the C.B.C. to give service to the people of Canada.
On the other hand the primary duty of the members of the Canadian association of broadcasters, as private stations, is to make profits. After they make profits then the service may come. According to figures I have last year private radio made a little over $2,000,000, and this on a capital of some $8,250,000, or a return of about 25 per cent. The licence fees charged private radio were slightly under $40,000. obviously a quite inadequate sum. But. if the Canadian association of broadcasters are going to insist that the private stations are there to serve the people, then I think those private stations should be satisfied with a return on capital of ten per cent at the most, and let the balance revert to the treasury of the nationally owned broadcasting company so that still greater service may be given the people. If the government does not agree with that idea then I suggest that the licence fees ought to be stepped up appreciably.
I wan-t to make clear once again what was said last year and in previous years. We in the C.C.F. are not in favour of a state monopoly of radio. We wan-t to see private community stations run for the benefit of the community, and as long as they do that they are playing their part. Some community stations are run very capably and efficiently; with others the position is just the reverse. One of the efficient stations I -think of is CKRC in my own city of Winnipeg. Although the station is owned by the Sifton interests the management is enlightened. In

Canadian Broadcasting Act
few cases where the public interest is at stake and one approaches the management and asks for free time to explain the situation is that time not given. At election time, whether municipal, provincial or federal, the management will get the parties together and say, "There is a certain amount of time available. No matter how much money you have you cannot buy more time. Divide it up among yourselves," and each is given fair play. The management of that station. I repeat, is broadminded and fairminded. Unfortunately these conditions do not exist throughout the entire private industry.
There can be little doubt in the minds of impartial observers. I think, that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters would very much like to slit the throat of the C.B.C. from ear to ear. They may not have avowed that intention, but it is implicit in many of the things they have said. Heaven help Canada if private radio takes over control, if ever it does; naturally I hope it does not. The first thing the C.A.B. would do would be to concentrate on the audiences in urban areas, because there you have your most compact audiences; and the people in the rural areas would not get the services they get now. There would be the very minimum of service where small profits were to be made. Today the C.B.C. carries programmes which I have no d-oubt are worthless commercially, worthless from the point of view of earning money, but of tremendous value from the standpoint of cultural and political unity. I can hardly think that private radio would give us programmes of the same type.
In their campaign against the C.B.C. this year the Canadian Association of Broadcasters bought full-page advertisements in about seventy Canadian newspapers, in an attempt to discredit the government owned radio organization. I do not know how manj' thousands or tens of thousands of dollars the C.A.B. paid for those advertisements, but advertising on such a national scale is rather an expensive hobby. Furthermore the committee was given the results of a survey which purported to show that national radio was in disfavour in quite a number of provinces throughout Canada. When inquiries were made it was disclosed that those responsible for perhaps the financial arrangements behind this survey were Imperial Oil, Aluminum Limited. Canadian Industries Limited, Canadian General Electric and Northern Electric. I think it is reasonable to believe that the results of that survey might be somewhat suspect, in view of the sponsors.
Does the hon. member know the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation used the same survey themselves?

I do not know it; I am talking about one particular survey which still is somewhat suspect.
The suggestion has been made that there is nothing very far wrong in newspapers owning radio stations. I disagree with that. In the first place, on more than one occasion newspapers have distorted facts. For instance, when the Montreal Gazette came to print the story about the survey it omitted two provinces which showed that they were in favour of national radio. I do know the newspapers in my own home town somewhat better. There is the Winnipeg Tribune, a newspaper which is without either bowels or brains, but on occasions has some heart. Then there is the Winnipeg Free Press, owned by the Sifton interests, a paper which if it can posssibly go out of its way to distort, will do so. I cannot feel at all happy at the prospect of such papers owning and controlling radio stations. I think it is imperative for the sake of freedom in Canada that the air be kept in the hands of the people of Canada. So long as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation protects the interests of the people of Canada, just so long are we prepared to vote for measures such as this one.

Mr. Speaker, rising this afternoon to take part in the debate may I say first that this year for the first time it was my pleasure to be a member of the radio committee. I must say I found the deliberations of that committee most interesting, but I had many complaints to make before it, and I did not support the final report when it came before the committee.
I believe hon. members may accept the frank view that every member who speaks in this debate is speaking because of the experience he has had in respect of radio in his own district or province. That is no indictment against any principle or any trust he may have; but by the natural course of events every hon. member coming from any section of Canada is interested either in his local radio station or conditions in radio in the province from whence he came. So this afternoon I wish to make it clear that my remarks emanate from the experience I have had, coming from British Columbia. Today most members have the experience of speaking over the radio. That does not pertain to any one member, because all of us take whatever advantage we can from the use of the radio, and I believe all appreciate that opportunity.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

I believe it can be said, too, that we can be thankful we are not in a country where listening in over the air is either prohibited or forced upon us. The public have a well-established right-and properly so-whereby if they do not like a programme, by a slight twist of the wrist they can tune it out.
When Mr. Dunton, the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, rvas before the committee, I asked him if he placed any confidence or any reliance in the Elliott-Haynes survey, and he admitted that it was about as fair a report as one could get. I do not care what any member says or what views he holds with respect to radio; the fact is that we have now before us and we had before the committee evidence that, according to the Elliott-Haynes report, in most provinces the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have a smaller number of listeners on the air than the private stations.
Where?

British Columbia. I would not refer to these figures this afternoon were it not for the fact that. I asked Mr. Dunton when he was before the committee if the Elliott-Haynes report was a reliable one, and he said it was. As a matter of fact it is t.he only report we have with respect to radio listeners over the various stations in Canada.
The last report given before the committee showed that in September 1944, fonty-four per cent of the people were in favour of private radio and thirty-six per cent in favour of government radio. The latest report, that of February 1947, reveals that the number of listeners preferring private radio had increased .from forty-four per cent to 57-8 per cent, while those listening in on C.B.C. stations had decreased from thirty-six per cent in 1944 to 24-1 per cent in February 1947.
Any hon. member may get up and argue all day about the C.B.C. being a better system of radio. But in the final analysis the people of Canada are the best judges as to which system is t.he best. And until we get a better report, then the Elliott-Haynes or one which will contradict the one I have before me, then 1 say we must take it that- so far as most provinces are concerned, most of the radio minded people are listening to private radio stations rather than to the C.B.C.
I say that is a total answer-and you can argue all day about the merits or demerits of the present situation. I am speaking for and about the Canadian people. I am speaking on- the official poll taken, taken throughout Canada, not among members of the C.C.F., the Social Credit or Progressive Conservative parties, but from the Canadian people themselves. Until it is refuted, in my opinion that 
record is the record of radio listeners in Canada. I have an open mind as to whether we should have a board similar to the board of transport commissioners to control radio. I must confess that at first blush there appears to be a good deal of merit in having another board to which both the C.B.C. and private radio stations would have to go, and under whose control they would come. I am not going to offer a definite opinion at the present time because, as I say, my mind is open in the matter.
However I have in mind other boards we have set up in the past. I think particularly of t.he Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, and I am wondering if the people of Canada are receiving the protection which was intended when that board was first established. When it was set up a long time ago, the view of the then government, and of the people generally I believe, was that some such board was required to protect the interests of the Canadian people. Over the course of the years however the viewpoint, and outlook of that board has changed considerably until today I can say without fear of successful contradiction that the board of transport commissioners are looking after the interests of the railways and not those of the people of Canada generally.
Can one imagine a member of parliament rising up in debate and asking for reduced freight rates? Let him do so, and he will receive the answer I have received for the past eighteen years: "That is not a matter for parliament to decide; it is one for the board to decide." I am afraid if a board were set up for radio, in the course of a few years the public might aw'aken to the fact that it had an autocratic board sitting in some building in Ottawa, a board over which parliament had no control.
As I say, my mind is open in the matter. But I believe the time has come when there should be a thorough review of the entire radio situation. I believe I would go so far as to say another commission similar to the Aird commission should be established, and I will state why. When the Aird commission was set up, compared with what it is today, radio was in its infancy. Some twenty years have gone by since that commission made its report. By the way, I am wondering how many members have read the Aird report. I know many did at the time it was published, and perhaps some have since; but I make the plea that every member of the House of Commons get a copy of the Aird report and read it again. What will they find? They will find, as I have, that many of the recom-

Canadian Broadcasting Act
mendations made in that report have been thrown in the discard and have never been acted upon. When the Aird commission set out to examine into radio they went to many countries, among them Great Britain. If they went to Great Britain today I venture to say that they would not find as many people in favour of the B.B.C. as were in favour of it in 1928. Those are the reports I receive from Great Britain at the present time. When (hey visited the United States they went to only one point and they had not much to say about United States radio.
This afternoon I want to draw attention to some of the recommendations that were made and I am going to complain because some of those recommendations have not been carried out. One recommendation was that there should be seven 50,000 watt stations throughout Canada, and British Columbia was mentioned as one place where such a station should be located. What do I find on looking over the list? I find that all we have in British Columbia is a 5,000 watt station. It :s well known that you must have a powerful station to get into the interior over the mountains. There is one of these 50.000 watt stations in Watrous, Saskatchewan, one in Montreal. and one in Sackville. As I say, there is a 5,000 watt station in Vancouver and another one in Toronto. I claim that we have been ignored so far as the recommendations of that commission are concerned.
Let us look at other recommendations. When the Aird commission investigated radio in this country they envisioned every provincial government taking a vital part and being tied in with radio. Here is one recommendation the commission made:
That a provincial radio broadcasting director should be appointed for each province to have full control of the programmes broadcast by the station or stations located within the boundaries of the province for which he is responsible.
That commission had considerable respect for the private stations of that day. In order to keep the record clear I will read the next recommendation:
That high-power stations should be erected across Canada to give good reception over the entire settled area of the country during daylight; that the nucleus of the system should possibly be seven 50,000 watt stations; that supplementary stations of lower power should be erected in local areas, not effectively covered by the main stations, if found necessary and as experience indicates.
Then they envisioned national unity and education, not the education spoken of here but scholastic education. Before dealing with that particular recommendation I should like 83166-3531
to read1 the main three recommendations, because they are the foundation of my address this afternoon. They are:
(a)	the establishment of one or more groups of stations operated by private enterprise in receipt of a subsidy from the government;
(b) the establishment and operation of stations by a government-owned and financed company;
(c) the establishment and operation of stations by provincial governments.
It was recommended, first, that there should be a national company; second, that provincial radio directors should be appointed in the provinces, and, third, that a provincial advisory council should be set up. In addition it was recommended that seven 50,000 watt stations should be established across tihe country. But there is another recommendation that has never been carried out. It was recommended that the great northland of this country should be provided with radio. If anyone will look at the map presented to the committee by the C.B.C. lie will find that there are not many radio stations in the far north. Yet the Aird commission envisaged radio being provided1 for the remote districts of Canada and for all our people. The C.B.C. was established in 1936. but little has been done about the recommendation up to the present time.
At one of the sittings of the committee I asked for details of the expenditures in the various provinces, but no one could find out what, they were. British Columbia has not been provided with a 50.000 watt station and yet that province pays more by way of radio licence fees than the three maritime provinces and the Yukon together. Last year British Columbia paid $385,514 for radio licence fees, while the maritimes and the Yukon paid $345,538. In other words, British Columbia listeners paid $36,676 more than the listeners in the maritimes and the Yukon. Yret our people are receiving, I was going to say nothing, but they are receiving very little from the C.B.C. Most people in British Columbia are Listening either to United States stations or 'to the local private stations. I quoted to the committee figures obtained by EIliott-Haynes Limited, one of these companies which takes radio tests throughout the country'. These showed that so far as British Columbia was concerned more people were listening to private stations and to United States stations than to the C.B.C.
Why is this? There is no high pressure group making these people listen to those stations. A simple turn of the knob will get you the station you want. Some one this afternoon spoke about encouraging fine music. I would like to know who is responsible for
Canadian Broadcasting Act

some of these soap box plays we hear, these weepy plays that go on by the hour where you can hear women tearfully weeping all the time. There is always tearfully weeping all the time. Some of them go on by the hour. Is that considered to be educating the people?
Are those on the air?
Yes. Where do you think they would be?
I was wondering how the hon. member got to know about them. Did he listen to them?

I am out for education. I do not take things secondhand. I listened to them and I know that on one Sunday one went on for a whole hour, the weepiest play I have ever heard on a Sunday evening. When you protest to C.B.C. about these plays they tell you that they are receiving many favourable letters. They may receive letters, but just look at what they did when this committee inquiry was on. I accused them at the time, and I say so again. They were able to get a lot of their highly paid patrons to write articles all over the country on behalf of the C.B.C.
The private stations were accused this afternoon of carrying on a high pressure campaign, and I do not think that should have been in the report. However, nothing was said about the high pressure campaign put on by the C.B.C. through their well known commentators. They are not paid directly to put on a campaign like that, but they did it just the same. They wrote articles from one end of the country to the other. These men are receiving remuneration, and if you do not call that a high pressure campaign I would like to know what it is. Let us be fair. This thing is not all one sided. These men do not want to be cut off the C.B.C. list. They are all getting some money on the side from the C.B.C. and they are out to support C.B.C I would like to know who chooses these soap operas. I asked about a man by the name of Sinatra, but I am not going to go into that now.
I am rising to oppose this bill. Because of what I heard in the committee I cannot help but oppose it until this whole radio system is thoroughly investigated-not by a committee of the House of Commons; oh, no; not after what we witnessed in the committee this year. I know I will probably be looked upon possibly as a black sheep because of the independent stand. I am taking. I am not apologizing for that, but I say that until we have a thorough independent inquiry I hardly think it is fair to tax the people of Canada who do not have a radio $544,673.
Someone mentioned the difference between the government and parliament, and I am

glad he did that, because all members on this side at least, and cabinet ministers in particular know full well that the public blame the government for collecting the licence fees. There is hardly a member of parliament, on this side at least, who if he is honest will not tell you that he has received criticism of the collecting of the licence fee and that it is aimed directly at the government. It is all very well to say that C.B.C. is under the control of parliament, but the government is linked up with the collecting of the licence fees. The collecting of the licence fees, in the mind of the public, is done by the government, because the Department of Transport is a department of the government, and therefore any grievance is laid at the door of the government, as well as enforcement and prosecutions. The government is held to blame for all that. None of us will say that we would like prosecutions to take place on the eve of an election. We might as well be frank, and I am bringing this point up to show that the government has some responsibility in this matter.

It is a good job that
there is one honest Liberal I know of.
Well, thanks.

I am sorry this short debate
is not going over the air. To come back to what I was saying before I was interrupted, there are in Canada something like 4.000.000 families, out of a population of approximately
12,000,000, who could have a radio licence. The radio licence fees collected this year, however, amounted only to $1,807,824. Roughly speaking, about fifty per cent of the householders have a radio licence. It has been a surprise to me that in proportion to our population we have far fewer homes in Canada with a radio licence than most other countries. Be that as it may, I think it is most unfair to tax the people who have no radios this 8544,673.	1 am going to oppose that.
I propose that the whole matter of radio be investigated by an independent commission of some kind and in the light of present modern inventions. Take .the question of facsimile newspapers, for instance, which came before the radio committee. The Aird commission on radio had no idea that facsimile newspapers would ever come into being.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
Again in regard to some other modern developments I do not think that C.B.C. is taking the proper attitude. Take television. I know that we have a marvellous heritage here. I know that some control will have to be exercised to prevent multiple ownership from becoming too great and becoming, shall I say, the entire boss of what goes over the air in this country. But parliament can impose proper safeguards. C.B.C. claims that it has not the funds to develop television. But private interests are ready to go ahead with it. I would not be so afraid of giving them the right to develop facsimile provided that we have proper regulations. We should not let C.B.C. sit there with a charter for television without supplying a television service, and simply holding the charter as a monopoly. 1 know that we must be careful not to allow private radio companies to control an entire chain from one end of this country to the other. I am against that kind of control or monopoly.
I am opposed therefore to increasing the amount of money to be given to C.B.C. by this scheme of turning over to them the whole of the licence fee. One other matter before I finish. If there were in Ottawa some private radio stations which were really alive to what the people want, I am sure that the people of Canada would be enjoying from time to time a programme from this city which only a few around here ever hear, and that is the programme from the carillon in the tower. Sometimes you can hear the bells from Big Ben in London over B.B.C.. but here in Ottawa unless you are within hearing distance of the tower in the House of Commons, you cannot enjoy the carillon programmes. If the C.B.C. had been alert to giving real service they would have allowed the entire country to hear that programme from the tower at least once a week, and in that way the rest of Canada who rontribute hundreds of thousands of dollars to C.B.C. could enjoy the carillon programme.
They might hear your bagpipes instead.

That would still be better than Sinatra. I am willing to bet that they would get more letters of commendation about the bagpipes than they would about Sinatra. Having given my views, Mr. Speaker, I simply say in conclusion that I am opposed to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy that the opportunity is presented to us to discuss the radio situation in Canada. I take a conscientious interest in my work and I would have been sadly disappointed had the radio committee's report been presented to parliament with no opportunity whatsoever for our discussing it.
Might I remind the house that while the radio committee's report was made to parliament, it was not unanimous; and furthermore, the report will not be concurred in by this house. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation take great delight in referring to the recommendations of previous parliamentary committees. The psychological effect of that lends the impression that parliament has approved of such-and-such and the corporation is acting in accordance with the wishes of parliament. But that is not so. What the corporation is acting upon when it says that it is doing so and so because of the recommendations of a radio committee of parliament is this: it is acting upon the recommendation of a few government members, some of whom will admit that they are not exceptionally well qualified in radio matters.
The setting up of a separate regulatory body seems to be the main theme of the pres-sentation by the independent stations throughout Canada. The report itself lays stress, through the use of a little phrase, on something which I think is receiving too much prominence. The report says:
They-
Referring to the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, representing some ninety odd stations in Canada:
They were insistent that any such organization-
Referring to a separate regulatory body.
-must be set up by the parliament of Canada as a whole-
I am not finding fault with that,, because a body would not be set up except by an act of parliament; but they continue, and this, is what I take exception to:
-and appointments to it should be by parliament of Canada as a whole and any review of its actions must be by parliament as a whole.
I think that is put in there for the purpose of discrediting the recommendations of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. I do not believe that the independent stations are necessarily pressing for individual appointment to such a board as having the necessity of receiving approval by this parliament. Their main theme is-and it is just as reasonable as anything could ever be-that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by its very nature should not be in a position where it can regulate and control its competitors. That is the main theme, and therefore an independent body responsible to parliament should be set up.
Canadian Broadcasting Act

I was happy to hear the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) say that his mind was still open on the subject of an . independent body. He did emphasize that he would not be in favour of an independent body that could rule the roost and not be responsible to parliament. Let me say to him that nobody has ever suggested such a body as that, not even the independent stations. We believe that any regulatory body should be responsible to parliament. That is only common sense. If the hon. member's mind continues to be open I for one am quite satisfied that he will eventually recommend the same thing that most of us are recommending, namely, that a separate regulatory body responsible to parliament should act as referee in matters of regulation between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-which, after all, is. we can say what we like, a government owned institution-and the private stations in Canada.
Mention is made of the fact that the Canadian daily newspapers' association supported that view. No comment is made. It is simply said that they supported that view. The Canadian daily newspapers' association is composed of 110 separate daily newspapers in Canada. That is worthy of consideration. They are supporting an independent body. The Canadian daily newspapers association is not vitally interested in radio as part of the .general set-up of newspapers. What they are mainly interested in is that radio itself is a *medium of disseminating information, education and news, and any institution with that great power should not be able to control its competitors. That is the main theme of all ihose who are supporting an independent body.
In the report I find a paragraph which "begins like this:
Your committee has given very careful consideration to the proposals for a separate regulating board.
I want the house to notice these words:
Your committee has given very careful consideration . . .
Mr. Speaker, that is just a laugh; that is a huge laugh. The committee did not give any consideration, let alone any careful consideration. to the setting up of an independent board. Someone might well ask, "Were you not on the committee?" Certainly I was on the committee, and I want to say this. I was also on the steering committee and I was a very busy man. I say that when we met there was no weighing of the evidence of those who presented their case for an independent body and that of those who presented any opposition to it. There is very good reason why {Mr. Hansel;.]
there was no weighing of the evidence. No evidence was presented in support of opposition to an independent body. When the committee gathered together in executive council to formulate a report I happened to be a very busy man. I had another committee meeting approximately at the same time. I came down to the house in the morning in a big hurry and I had not even shaved. That does not make any difference as far as coming down to the house is concerned. But as time went on I did not even have time to have anything to eat at noon. That does not make any difference either. But when at about 4.30 o'clock I went into the committee which was supposed to weigh all the evidence there was hardly a quorum there. Therefore I said to the chairman, "Well, this is one time when I shall be very valuable to you. I will stay at least until you get a quorum." He looked at me and I could see what he was looking at, because I was looking like an African Santa Claus. I had not had time yet either to shave or eat. I stayed until the quorum came. Then I said. "What is the agenda?" The agenda was read through and the separate regulatory body was at the end of the agenda. I said, "Well, Mr. Chairman, I think I can snatch five minutes to go down and get a sandwich and a cup of coffee." The chairman said, "Yes, I think you can." I rushed down and had a sandwich and a cup of coffee, and when I came back to the committee half of the members had gone and the other half were picking up their papers ready to leave. I said. "Mr. Chairman, is it all over?" He said, "Yes, we have the whole thing fixed up." I said, "What did you do about this independent board?" He said, "Oh, they sat on it; they quashed it completely; they would not have anything to do with it." I said, "Well, I am surprised. I thought the intelligence of this committee was higher than that." What I am putting over to the house now is that that is how carefully they weighed and considered the evidence which was presented for an independent board.
