Will the minister himself above anyone else, question my attitude toward the setting-up of an independent board. I was in the committee. Of course I was, and when the time came, when the entire committee was there, I was ready to emphasize the need of an independent board. That is why I made certain it was at the last of the agenda.
Does not silence mean consent?

Not when you are not there. The point I make is that this is the careful way in which they went into the weighing of the evidence. Evidence is not weighed between the views of one and the views of another. People make up their minds, and I will go farther than that. My belief is that sometimes people's minds are made up for them before there is an opportunity of weighing evidence.
Now here is something in this report that I w'ould bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker. I am going to say, before I quote it, that this part is false and I objected to it at the time. It appears in the same paragraph:
Your committee has given very careful consideration to the proposals for a separate regulating board and has also received numerous arguments from other bodies such as trade unions, agricultural organizations, cooperative societies, and the like, in opposition to those proposals, to which also the committee has given careful consideration.
What is the truth of that paragraph? In the first place, the way the paragraph reads is that numerous arguments were received. Anyone reading it would think these organizations came before tihe committee. They
did not come before the committee. They submitted letters to the committee. The letters were read and appear as an appendix to the evidence. They can be read in report No. 11. But what I want to say is this, that this opposition which seemed to come from these trade unions, agricultural organizations and cooperative societies, is not in fact the truth, and I will challenge the minister or anyone in the committee to read these letters and find more than one place where these organizations stated that they oppose a separate regulatory body. What they do say is that they are satisfied with the present radio policy and some of them are pulling for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That is all right; that is their privilege. But to say that their arguments against a regulatory body were carefully considered is more than foolish nonsense. It is false.
While that is put in there, no mention is made of the other letters that were received supporting the Canadian Association of Broadcasters in their desire for a separate regulatory body. No mention is made of those, and there were letters from other organizations to that effect.
There is another matter along this line. It is a strange thing that no arguments are used as to why a separate regulatory body should not be set up. There are those who say it is not needed. There are those who say they are satisfied with things as they are. But no arguments are ever advanced as to why a separate board should not be set up. When we ask in what way the effectiveness of broadcasting by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would be lessened, no arguments are presented. When we sav, "Well, if there is an independent body, tell us how that, would affect in any way the efficiency of the broadcasting of the C.B.C.?" No arguments are presented. A separate body does not mean that radio will be any Iks effective. It only means that there will be a referee and that one competitor cannot control the other.
I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), who gushed forth in vitriolic vein, with some considerable push, a multiplicity of puny arguments. He vigorously defends state monopoly of radio, and the reason is that it serves the socialist purpose. It is significant that in his speech he did not present one argument why a separate regulatory body should not be set up. I am not surprised, because there are no arguments. I am very happy that he has had an opportunity to do so much radio broadcasting. I believe he said he had broadcast about 900 times. One thing is certain, that radio has been especially good to him, and if he can say that some of
Canadian Broadcasting Act

his broadcasts were given over C.B.C., all I can say is that C.B.C. has been a little kinder to him than it has been to most of us.
I am convinced of this, Mr. Speaker. After sitting on the radio committee for a good many years, I am convinced that we shall never get a separate regulatory body until there is a change in government. That is the conclusion I have reached. We can say all we want about non-interference by the government. I am not going to charge them with any interference. It is certain, however, that radio policy in Canada today is government radio policy, and we shall not have any independent board or referee until there is a change in government.
I am not going to elaborate this point, but in the report a whole paragraph is devoted to a campaign which was carried on by the independent stations during the time the committee was meeting. Well, in the steering committee I objected to that paragraph being included. I agree that perhaps it was a special spurt on the part of the independent stations to inform the public; and why not? Anybody has that right in Canada; it is still a free country. No one will say that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not done similar things in days gone by. I do not know how many newspaper advertisements it has published, but I will say that tons of literature have gone out in support of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Nothing is said of that. I am not objecting to it; it is something that is to be expected. Furthermore-and I am saying this complementary to what the hon. member for New Westminster said- ho-w about last year, when circular letters were sent out by the farm forum to all their farm forum groups? I know the argument will be that the C.B.C. did not do that. Well,
I am going to tell you there is quite an affinity between the farm forum organization and the C.B.C. They sent out circular letters with resolutions the same word for word, sending them through the mails or placing them on; the desks of the secretaries of all these farm forums with a request that they send them in to the radio committee, whether or not they knew very much about radio. That was quite a high pressure campaign, and perhaps more effective than any newspaper campaign.
With respect to revenues, the committee reports that the independent stations are making some considerable profits. 1 am not going to say they are not profit-making institutions. In our system of private enterprise what business institution is not a profit-making institution? They would not stay in business 
very long if they were not. But when we talk about private enterprise and profit, let us remember it is not only a profit system we are living under; it is a profit and loss system. Radio stations can lose money, too. I am not saying many of them are losing money now, and I am glad they are not. I do not begrudge anyone a profit if it is not exorbitant and stolen from somebody else. I will challenge anyone to prove how the consumers of products or the Canadian people are suffering any loss from their own pocket-books through the profit that independent stations may be making from their commercial and advertising business.
Who pays for it?
My hon. friend raises the same question as he raised last year: "Who pays for it?" The people who buy the goods.
We have to eat soap with our breakfast.
I will say this, that by reason of the advertising done by radio a product can be sold in such quantities that in all probability the public pays less for it.
Ho. ho.

Anyone who says "Ho, ho" to that statement reveals his ignorance. I would advise these men, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), to be a little careful how they speak of the great and mighty profits that independent stations are making, because if they are not careful they are going to overdo it. Somebody is going to ask them how it is, then, if radio is such a profitable business, that the C.B.C. goes into the red. They have to be careful not to ride that horse too hard. I want to be fair. I know the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is required to meet huge expense; I am not denying that. I know they spend a great deal of money on programmes. I know they spend a lot of money in the search for talent. I know all about that, and I do not begrudge them a cent that is used properly. Let that be understood. Nevertheless I say that the argument goes both ways. If radio is such a profitable business, what is the position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, having a tremendous advantage to start with, having four or five million dollars handed to them from the Canadian taxpayers, not having to pay any taxes as the independent stations must pay? So I say that those who argue against the profits being made by independent stations should be very careful.
There is another little matter I should like to bring before the committee, because it

Canadian Broadcasting Act
affects a radio station within radio distance of my own constituency, and I think one has a right to speak in the interests of his own people. It has to do with the matter of free expression. Some evidence was brought out by the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. to the effect that sometimes independent stations were not paying enough attention to free speech on the air. The station involved in the argument was the- voice of the prairies station, CFCN, in Calgary. An extract was read from a letter in proof-and I want you to mark this, Mr. Speaker-of the suggestion that some independent stations were not paying enough attention to free speech on the air. This is what was quoted from the letter, and I think I will read the comment as well:
The following, for instance, is from a letter received from station CFCN, Calgary. This station is a prominent member of the C.A.B., the most powerful private station west of Winnipeg, and its representatives before the committee last year spoke hotly about freedom of the air for the people of Alberta. The letter said:
"As C.B.C. regulations require a station to sell time to all groups, if they sell to any (distribute time fairly), we have discontinued selling time between elections for political broadcasts, because about the only people who would spend money fifty-two weeks in the year belonged to some 'ism' or other."
I say that was unfair. It did not give the entire picture. The witness went on to say:
This is hard to reconcile with statements in the C.A.B. brief about freedom of the air . . .
What was the case; what was the letter? I do not have the full file; no doubt the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has it all. I got in touch with the station and I said, "What is this all about?" They sent me the letter from which this was quoted. What had happened? I shall show first of all, that only that part of the letter which suited the argument of the C.B.C. was quoted. I shall begin by reading the first paragraph, to show that it is a friendly letter addressed to Mr. Dan
E.	Cameron of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at Winnipeg. It starts out, "Dear Dan."-so it is friendly, you see-
We acknowledge yours of May 14th with regard to the origination of "Terry Levis" talk on Tuesday May 20th from CFCN.
Then, later on, the paragraph from which the quotation is made reads this way:
Had we accepted the revenue tender to us by various representatives of communism, socialism and other various "isms," at $40 per quarter-hour (money subscribed by their sucker following, if the broadcast is sufficiently bombastic), we could have taken a good many hundred dollars, but as C.B.C. regulations require a station to sell time to all groups, if they sell to any (distribute time fairly), we have discontinued selling time between elections for political broadcasts because about the only people who would spend money 52 weeks in the year belonged to some "ism" or other.
What was the reason for it? As a matter of fact, on one occasion I consulted this station, because I had been asked by my group if I would see the manager of CFCN for the purpose of purchasing time on the air for our Social Credit group. What did the manager say? He said, "We can- sell you time but, as a matter of fact, we have just finished- an election, and we think that perhaps the people are a little bit tired of political broadcasts." He persuaded me that that was not the right time to make political broadcasts.
What happened in this instance to which Mr. Dunton referred? No Progressive Conservative organization was asking to buy time; no Social Credit organization was asking to buy time; no Liberal organization was asking to buy time; but the communists and those of socialist views were pressing for time on the air. The station could have sold it at $40 a clip for fifty-two weeks in the year. In order to maintain a perfect balance, the radio stations said, "Well, for a time at least we will cut out all political broads casts."
That is reasonable, but it is not the way it appears in the evidence. In the evidence it would appear as though this radio station were refusing to present all sides of the case. The very thing they were trying to do was, if possible, to present all sides of the case; and if they could not get all sides of the case they would, not -broadcast any.
That is the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At page 404 of the proceedings of the committee I find that the horn, member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight), a well respected member of that committee, asked about freedom of speech on the air, and he was asking particularly if labour unions had had an opportunity of going on the air. The chairman of the board of governors answered in this fashion:
In our general policy regarding opinion broadcasting on our own networks we try, as our white paper says, to give a chance for different viewpoints to be expressed.
That is all the station in Calgary wasr doing. The paragraph is snitched from its context and used in an attempt to prove that private radio does not believe in free speech. That is unfortunate.
In respect of talent we have heard the suggestion that private radio should give more time to live talent and in the seeking out and nurturing of passible Canadian artists. I have no objection to that; no one has. But let me say this:	I would suggest that the

Canadian Broadcasting Act
independent- stations are doing just as much as is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in finding talent. Let us remember that radio does not make talent; it discovers it. Radio cannot afford to lose audiences by putting amateurs who are not acceptable on the air to the public.
There is the question in my mind as to whether the more important function of radio is to give the people what they want, within the scope of reasonable and respectable culture, or whether its function is that of the schoolroom. I am not convinced that it is the function of radio to train radio artists. I believe it is radio's function to discover artists; the schoolrooms, the dramatic societies and organizations of that kind are the ones which make them. I do not believe there is one amateur programme put over the air by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. but many independent stations hold amateur contests. I believe, if the whole story were told, it would be found that the private stations are doing a fair job in encouraging local talent. If an artist is worth anything he is soon discovered by radio; make no mistake about that. The schoolroom, the private music teacher, the band leaders, the dramatic critics, the schools of fine arts and institutions of that sort are the ones which make the talent; radio finds it.

speechtext: Not yet.

Perhaps my words are prophetic. I will retract them for the time being and say "the hon. member for Eglinton." I should like to associate myself also with a large part of what has been said by the hon.
[Mr. Hansell.1
member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). I feel that the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have perhaps been more marked by attempts to expand the fields of their endeavour than to improve the quality- some of them are excellent-of the programmes which they present to the Candian public.
However I wish to deal with the terms of the bill. I think it can be admitted, without scandalizing either parliament or the Canadian public, that the government cannot administer as economically as can private enterprise. There may be reasons why administration by government is always much more costly than by private enterprise, but that is not a reason for not keeping accurate accounts of what those costs are. The bill before us is a short one. It proposes to substitute a new paragraph for paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 14 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act. The original subsection is in these words:
The Minister of Finance shall deposit from time to time in the Bank of Canada or in a chartered bank to be designated by him to the credit of the corporation:-
(a) the moneys received from licence fees in respect of private receiving licences and private station broadcasting licences, after deducting from the gross receipts the cost of collection and administration, such costs being determined by the minister from time to time.
It is sought to replace that subsection with the following:
The Minister of Finance shall deposit from time to time in the Bank of Canada or in a chartered bank to be designated by him to the credit of the coporation:-
(a) the gross amount of the moneys received in each year from licence fees in respect of private receiving licences and private station broadcasting licences without deducting therefrom any costs of collection or administration.
The result is that there is to be deposited to the credit of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the amount collected without deducting the cost of effecting that collection. The explanatory note to the bill tells us that last year the cost of collecting approximately $4 million was $544,673.17. I consider that that cost is too high and altogether out of proportion to what it should be. I am certain that, did the government place the collection of this money in private hands, it could be collected for at least one-half the present cost and the collector would still make a handsome profit. It is to be remembered that a substantial proportion of these moneys are paid through the post office without even the cost of a notice.
The bill means that the science of accountancy is to be dispensed with so far as it is

Canadian Broadcasting Act
applied to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This is disturbing. Part of the actual cost of operation is no longer to be shown in the accounts of that corporation. This is not only a violation of the great science of accountancy; it is a violation of the elements of good business, of fair dealing and of keeping faith with the public. The only reason for keeping accounts is to enable all and sundry to know at all times exactly what a business is spending and exactly what it is receiving. The sole purpose of this bill is to strike from the accounts of this broadcasting corporation one of the principal costs of doing business. It is a method of subsidizing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in a hidden and utterly improper way.
My hon. friends who sit to my left remind us quite frequently-and we have heard it today-that in their view there is some impropriety in private broadcasting companies making profits. We have heard those private enterprises criticized severely because they made profits. I ask myself whether it is more reprehensible to make profits than it is to conceal losses. I would think that the conscience which dictates disapproval of profits, whether or not they be excessive, would be highly critical of legislation which can have but one result, whatever its purpose, that, of deceiving the Canadian people.
We have been told by the minister that broadcasting in this country is much more expensive than it is in other countries. He gave what I thought was a sound reason for this, the tremendous area over which word has to be carried through the ether and sparsity of our population. He went on to explain that the licence fee in Canada is but $2.50. whereas in England it is a pound or, roughly, $5, and. if my memory serves me well, twenty-five shillings in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, or about $6. I am going to suggest to the minister that, if what he has stated is accurate, it is only right that our radio licence fee should be raised. If the sparsity of our population and the dimensions of the area in which we are attempting to carry on radio business makes the per capita cost higher in Canada than in the other lands, the natural and inevitable thing to do is to raise the cost of the licence fee. I admit I hat that would not be popular; but an honest man. even to satisfy the requirements of his own conscience, sometimes has to do things that are not altogether popular. If the cost of the broadcasting service in this country comes to $3 per head instead of $2.50, let us exact that $3 instead of $2.50 from the holder of a radio set. But let us not introduce into
this great undertaking an element of deceit which no man would tolerate for a moment in his own business and which is bound to create dissatisfaction and distrust in regard to the broadcasting corporation. It will also engender abuses. We all know that in public undertakings costs inevitably increase; the number of people employed inevitably increases. So it goes on year after year, and the burden of taxation becomes continually heavier. It is only by carefully scrutinizing all expenditures and by knowing exactly the reasons for them that we can hope to keep them under control.
I suggest to the minister-and he is not a man without experience in business-that he would not tolerate for a moment a method of accounting similar to that which is embodied in the amendment now before us, in any private enterprise of which he was a director or over which he had any control. I submit that it is almost an affront to the Canadian public to tell it that it is incapable of understanding that the cost of a certain service is greater than that which is being charged for it and that some devious way must be found in order to make up to the corporation the loss which it has incurred. To my knowledge, excepting possibly the hidden subsidies that were resorted to as a matter of expediency during the war, there has never been anything like this offered to the Canadian public before, unless it be the statute introduced some years ago whereby several hundred millions of debt of the Canadian National Railways was legislated out of existence. That I do not think was a very happy occasion.
I do not think the procedure was ever justified. I do not think it was a precedent that is worthy of being followed, especially in the early days of the development of one of the great agencies for influencing public opinion and forming character, one of the great educative and cultural agencies of the land. It should be kept as free as possible of anything which savours of impropriety or deceit.
I submit that this bill introduces into the affairs of the Broadcasting Corporation a flavour of duplicity and double-dealing that is not at all attractive, and I sincerely hope that the minister will tear up the bill and raise the licence fee to $2.75 or $3, if necessary, or bring in frankly and openly a bill in aid to make up the operating deficit of the corporation. But let us have none of the petty methods that are suggested by the bill before us.

Mr. Speaker,
I have been on the radio committee for a good many years, and I do not see any differ-
Canadian Broadcasting Act

ence 'between this radio committee and others on which I have sat. It has always been the same way. We have always had the old steam-roller, the socialist and semi-socialist Liberals with their majority on the committee, so that there is really not much use in suggesting anything with respect to the report.
The hon. minister took the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) to task for not objecting to some of the items in the committee's report. One has only to read the report to see how unsatisfactory it is. I objected to the figures of profits being included in the report, but. the committee would not stand for my objection. I do not think it is right to publish these figures on profits such as these, because it does not give any kind of picture of the whole show. I do not object to these stations making profits. I think that the more profits they make, the more talent they will have and the more advertising they can do, and the more labour that will create.
So far as any careful consideration of the proposal in the bill is concerned, I do not think there was any proper consideration given to it. When these reports are being prepared I think it should be done in open session, so that the public can come and see how the different members of the committee feel on these various questions. Then we would get some results.
The report was not unanimous, and we can easily understand that. I am free to admit that there are some parts of the report with which I agree, but I should like to say that the committee was late in being set up, and, after it was set up, it was late in being called together. Our deliberations were lengthy; a lot of witnesses had to be called, and the work of the committee was hurried toward the end, so that we did not really have time to go into some matters that we should have liked to go into. There were a great many statistics and briefs placed before us, and they came so quickly that it was almost impossible to read and become familiar with them.
I agree with the report that a standing committee of this house should be set up. The whole question of radio is far more important than the question of money involved in connection with it. There were certain things that the committee did not take into consideration at all. While I was on the committee, it seemed to me that any proposals which were ever made by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters the majority of the members of the committee tried to discredit. The report almost seems to indicate, as the hon. member for Macleod said, that organizations such as agricultural organizations, coop-

erative societies and trade unions were heard. One trade union appeared before us and was examined, the musicians' union. That was the only union which came before us to be questioned. From that point of view the report is not correct.
The purpose of this bill is to give the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the whole of the $2.50 licence fee extracted from radio owners. It is proposed to give them the whole without taking away the cost of collection. In other words, the owner of a radio is to be taxed thirty cents for the privilege of paying $2.50. That is what it amounts to. Since nationally owned radio was established in 1932 there has been a radio fee. First of all a fee of $2 was collected from the owner of each radio with the exception of blind people. In 1937 the revenue was $1,750,000. In the fall of that year the fee was raised to $2.50 for ordinary sets and to $2 for battery sets. These fees were collected on account of each radio owned by every person. In 1940, in response to a political move to abolish the radio fee, it was decided to collect a fee only from each home or multiple dwelling which includes, I suppose, each person who has a radio in a boarding house or each person who has a radio in a dwelling or multiple dwelling or each person who has a radio in a hotel room. The C.B.C. now receive $3,905,841, as well as $1,900,000 from advertising. The excuse for raising the fee to $2.50 in 1938 was given by the minister of transport of that date as follows:
It is not the desire or the intention of the corporation at any time to obtain a revenue over $500,000 from commercial sources for reasons that are obvious.
It has gone up nearly four times that amount since that time, to $1,800,000. That amount of $500,000 was considered to be in the public interest at that time for reasons that are obvious. I do not know what the obvious reasons are now.
If this bill passes, as I suppose it will, it will be to all intents and purposes, as was stated, a subsidy from the public purse to the extent of the cost of collection. There is no doubt about that. In my opinion it is only a matter of time before the C.B.C. will face another emergency and will come back and want more money. To my mind the bill is hardly an honest bill. The government should not have asked parliament to pass the bill under these circumstances. I would suggest that there are two honest ways of meeting the problem. The first one is to raise the radio licence fee to the required amount and thus put a halt to this confusion, or to put

Canadian Broadcasting Act
the whole thing on a direct basis and let parliament take the full responsibility now. The public would then know the cost. Parliament should be responsible for the expenditure of the money by the C.B.C. It would be far more economical than it is at the present time, and it would certainly be less irksome to the individual licence owner.
As I have said before in the house, why should a person who has one radio pay as much as a person who has twenty? The situation is ridiculous. Why should not the person who listens be taxed? He is the person who gets the advantage. Just because a person has a radio it does not seem to me to be any reason why the radio should be licensed. As I have said before, we might just as well license refrigerators or washing machines. The owners of these machines use electricity and get service. Why should you not license them? If you are going to license at all, license the listener by taking the money out of the consolidated revenue fund.
Here is the situation. If it is right to collect a licence fee of $2.50, then it is right to raise the licence fee to $3, if necessary. Of course that would not be politically popular. Perhaps that is the answer. If it is right to raise thirty-five cents, or $554,000, at the expense of the consolidated revenue fund, it is right to raise all the money at the expense of that fund through taxes.
Let us see what the situation is. The sum of $4,406,964 was collected. The cost of collection was $547,700. or a cost of thirty-five cents a licence because there were 1,807,824 licensees. The net amount given to the C.B.C. was $3,905,841. The. cost of collecting that amount of money was fourteen per cent of the amount collected. It is absurd to have a cost of collection of that amount by a government which calls itself responsible for the taxpayers' money. I understand that the cost of collecting all the revenue in Canada amounts to less than eight-tenths of one per cent. Why spend $554,000 of the taxpayers' money when the collection could be made for so much less?
In addition to that, there were 11,621 prosecutions. How absurd it is to bring 11,624 people to court to get $2.50 from each of them and the court costs as well. Some 11,624 people were prosecuted, or six-tenths of one per cent of the licences issued. Sixty-seven per cent of these were in Ontario, where only thirty-four per cent of the licences were issued, and ten per cent in Quebec, where twenty-six per cent of the licences were issued. It is obvious, on that basis, that the policing of the licences is not being done equally all over the country.
That goes for the other provinces as well. I am not singling out Quebec, or anything like that. How many other people living in houses or multiple dwellings having radios have not bought their licences? I do not know, but there are over a million and one-half people in the metropolitan areas of Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Hamilton. How in the world can one expect to find out whether these people have paid their licence fee or not? The thing on the face of it is ridiculous.
This is a majority report of the Liberal members of the House of Commons, backed by the C.C.F. That is true. There are none so blind as those who will not see, and little progress has been made consistently with our democratic principles so far as this report is concerned. We still have the same feature that has dominated other reports; that is, continued allegiance to political questions. The report is purely political. Consideration of principles-freedom of the air, equity and justice, the use of the radio for communication-have almost been forgotten in the report. The report implies, as a matter of fact, that there was little purpose in the committee continuing the hearing, since the majority have no interest in analysing complaints or weighing the merits of the representations made.
There is one fundamental principle that has been before the committee many times before, and that is in connection with the monopoly of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is a monopoly which has authority arbitrarily to regulate each radio outlet and each voice of the nation. What was new was the still stronger case made by the Canadian daily newspapers association, which added its voice to that of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. Something was said in the committee to the effect that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters had no complaint, that they did not think they had a complaint, that they were in a happy position. I simply ask this question:	Why, then, did they take the
trouble of submitting a brief and having so many of their associations here waiting, watching and giving evidence if necessary? I will tell you why. It was because the association of broadcasters and the private stations themselves feel that the sword of Damocles hangs over their heads all the time, represented by the C.B.C. The report shows what little attention has been given to the brief in reference to the aforesaid matters. It is true that a certain amount of lip service has been given to it, but the very fact that one of the private stations had its head cut off by this totalitarian corporation-because that is what it is-
Canadian Broadcasting Act

after years of toil and after years of work from the early stages of experimentation, and the progress it has made, shows that there is certainly something that needs fixing up. Their head was cut off-why? Because of the splendid audience they have built up. This shows the injustice of the present system. Whether it was legal or not, this act on the part of the dictators would not, to my way of thinking, have been allowed had an independent regulatory and licensing body been functioning. That alone, to my mind, and, I believe, to the minds of most thinking people, shows the necessity of such a body being set up.
Not only that; but time after time, in the radio committee, it has been pointed out that the arbitrary rules of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have been a great detriment to Canada. Evidence has been given to that effect. Because of the negligence, perhaps selfishness, on the part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; perhaps because of overpaternalism in refusing licences; because of regulations done away with only after the last session of the committee, and the decision to allow them to increase their power from one kilowatt maximum to five kilowatt maximum, which was put into force only last year; because many of the channels that should have been occupied were refused occupancy by the arbitrary decision of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; because power has been denied these stations for many years-for all these reasons, Canada has lost the full use of a great many channels which could have served the public.
May I point out that the silly thought that there are only two classes of radio broadcasting in Canada is nonsense. There are three classes. There are stations which do national chain broadcasting, the high-powered stations; there are the community stations, the lower-powered stations, from 250 to 500 or 1,000 watts; and there is the station which is far more important, which gets the greatest coverage, namely the regional station. The public of Canada have been denied more regional stations because of the arbitrary action of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in refusing to allow them to go, in some cases, up to fifty kilowatts and, in some cases, from five to ten.
In days gone by, our stations would have served the country much better if they had been allowed to go to their full power; and the C.B.C. regulations in restricting them to any power arbitrarily fixed, without regard to proper occupancy of channels, has resulted in a considerable loss to Canada. Possibly there is . some opportunity for Canadian stations to

increase their power even now. Unfortunately, however, that opportunity has largely disappeared. Many channels, as I said before, have been lost through arbitrary rules of the C.B.C. in not allowing licences to new stations for wave lengths in the past.
As an example of what I have said, and to support it, I will quote' a few lines from what Professor Bayly said the year before last and also last year with reference to the loss of stations and power and the consequent loss of coverage to Canada. Time after time we have been told in the radio committee that we have not lost any coverage and have not lost any channels. We know that we have lost channels, and the evidence of Professor Bayly, a distinguished engineer who has received fine decorations, cannot be gainsaid. This is what he said before the radio committee in 1945 and again in 1946. at page 432:
Everybody is interested in raising their power and to put a better signal into the area, but I point out that actual engineering figures on these areas are surprisingly small, and I think that after the war is finished and we get the completion of the occupation of the frequencies on the Havana agreement we will be perturbed as to how small our coverage is, especially at night.
Later on, he said:
. . . the policy which has been adopted here of keeping stations down to low power instead of having them up to their minimum power under the Havana agreement has had a detrimental effect on the coverage which we can expect in the future for the people of Canada.
This situation should be corrected before we have any further trouble. There should1 be some tribunal which is able to judge on the merits of the case after.calling witnesses, and to decide whether the propositions put before them are right or wrong. You just cannot help it when you are in the position of the C.B.C. Again Professor Bayly says:
. . . a great many regional stations are now permitted five kilowatts, but the tendency is still there. A very good example is the one 1 was quoting this morning. 1010, where if the present occupants, the C.B.C.. get off 1010 and another occupant comes in, they lose priority, and Canada as a whole, or that particular area of Canada, loses some of the available space on the spectrum that is available to Canada in the radio broadcasting band.
Surely that should be enough to convince anyone. The minister and those around him may laugh, but these are facts. Perhaps he should have a little greater interest in Canada and in service to the Canadian people. Perhaps I have a little more interest in it than he has; perhaps he does not know anything about it.. The situation is that the C.B.C., in conjunction with the radio branch of the Department of Transport, is the lawmaker,

Canadian Broadcasting Act
the law enforcer, the judge, the competitor and the policeman, as has been stated by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). I should like to point out also that in the whole of the C.A.B. brief I cannot find one word of criticism of the C.B.C. in regard to their broadcasting activities. As a matter of fact the Canadian Association of Broadcasters went so far as to say they did not mind any competition from the C.B.C., but they did object to the principle under which the broadcasting corporation was the competitor, the lawmaker and the law enforcer, judge and policeman. I do not blame them. I think something should be done about that, and very soon.
I should now' like to say a. word about commercialism. The report says action should be taken to compel private stations to devote greater attention to the development of public service features, while their tendency to overcommercialism should, be curbed. That is a laugh. The report further states that the private stations should use more local talent. I quite agree; but in the very nature of things. a9 everyone knows, a commercial station must be commercial. It cannot be overcommercial. All these stations put on some sustaining programmes, but they have to make a profit unless they are to go into the red. Perhaps then they would get government assistance, as the C.B.C. does. If they are to exist at all, certainly they must get fees from broadcasting. I do not see how a commercial radio station can be overcommercialized. The very fact that it has to seek an audience means that, of necessity, it has to put on some things which perhaps the sponsors may not want, but it has to keep an even balance. The audience is the thing that is necessary. This suggestion of overcommercialism is silly when you think of it in connection with the great C.B.C. I suppose they do no commercial work at all. From what I have read, they were supposed to have an income of only
S500.000	from commercial broadcasting; that was to be the limit. They got up to Sl.800.000. and at the present time forty-five per cent of their revenue comes from commercial broadcasting. They were supposed to be the people who would do the cultural work and carry the sustaining programmes, through the fees collected for licences. The report might better have been directed at the C.B.C. than at the private stations.
Then let us consider the latest programme of expansion proposed by the C.B.C. First of all, they intend to take over the wave length of CFRB. Why? For the sole purpose of having a key station. I asked why they wanted CFRB as a key station, and could not get very much of an answer except that they
had to have a high-powered station. What they really wanted was a key station which had a ready-made audience of from one and a half to two million people which had been built up by that station. As the hon. member for Eglinton has said, this is nothing but legalized robbery. They wanted also to be able to command a good price for advertising in order to bolster up their second network. Not commercial? Oh, no. If it is not commercial I do not know what is. Not only that; but after taking over CFRB, in all probability they will still have to occupy 1010, or we will lose it. They have 1010 now, which is quite sufficient for their purposes, but they want the advertising there, and what they are trying to do is to bring coals to Newcastle. The people in southern and central Ontario get good service now. They would have had better service if the arbitrary dictators of the C.B.C. board had not refused this station the opportunity to go to fifty kilowatts, which would have given them a good signal to serve the people of the communities in and around Toronto, as -well as more distant districts. What has actually happened is that the people of Canada have lost the coverage and the listening pleasures they might have had, as a result of that arbitrary action. An improvement could have been brought about there without any expense at all to the country, but now it will cost us this amount of money.
What is the picture as far as the C.B.C are concerned? They are going to take over CFRB. which is to cost $300,000. when the coverage might have been obtained without any expenditure. That money was voted last year. I suggest that $300,000 might have been more profitably used to do the job the C.B.C. was set up to do; that is, to give proper coverage to all the people of Canada, instead of setting up another station in a congested area which needs another high-powered station just about as much as a cow needs a fifth foot.
The report states that the deficit of the C.B.C. last year was $70,000. It should have been given as a great deal more than that, because no depreciation has been allowed for, and at least $297,000 should have been set up for depreciation. The budget proposals of this year showed a deficit of $265,000 but you have to add depreciation to get the true deficit. Anyone with any sense at all knows you must allow depreciation of ten per cent on equipment, of that kind. That would give a deficit of $492,000. so that, with this additional $544,000, the C.B.C. will just about get by.
The first job the C.B.C. was supposed to do was give coverage to all the people of Canada. That coverage should have been given
Canadian Broadcasting Act

by one chain, instead of biting off more than they -could chew by setting up another chain which was absolutely unnecessary to give service to the sparsely populated parts of the country that do not and cannot get service a't the present time. If necessary, this money Should be used to establish more stations in outlying -areas. Give all the listeners service; that is what we want of the broadcasting corporation. Instead of that, they are setting up this second chain -because they want the advertising revenue. In addition, they have done a little legalized robbery, as I said before, in order to get this key station. As a consequence, for some time to come -there will be parts of this country that will not have the coverage they should have. This has been done for the sake of advertising, I am referring to the second claim. One realizes just how facetious the report of the committee is when it states that the private broadcasting stations are not to over commercialize to any great extent, in the face of the fact that a non-commercial business C.B.C. gets forty-five per cent of its income from commercial business, something that was never anticipated under former circumstances.
Private stations are doing more than the C.B.C. are doing by way of developing talent. It can be said that they are doing just as much, anyway. And, so far as local service is concerned, the service they are giving is just as good. I am willing to give the C.B.C. more money to do the job of work i-t was set up to do, namely to cover every part of the country. But I am not willing to give them money -to spend in the closely congested centres of poulation where there is no need for any more service.
Then, private broadcasting stations have been refused the right to do chain broadcasts. I say they shouild be given that right, and should be allowed to buy their line service on a competitive basis with that of the C.B.C., although I agree the C.B.C. should have priority.
My reasons for saying that should be done are these: it would relieve the C.B.C. from some of its obligations in respect of coverage; it would' do a better job for the listening public; it would' increase the variety of programmes and, most important, it would give the people of Canada another voice. That is something which we must always keep in mind.
It is all very well to say that the C.B.C. is an independent corporation. While that may be true at the present time, there is a tremendous danger that it may not remain so in the future. The danger is there. We have plenty of voices in this chamber,, but the point

is to get these voices outside. To a great extent the C.B.C. have been fairly impartial in this respect, and I give them credit for it. The same can be said for the Canadian press. But the danger of only one voice in radio is still present, and unwarranted control of radio makes it all the more important that that, danger should be removed.
Radio broadcasting is greatly different from what it was when the first commission was established; it has grown, like Topsy. To my mind, now is the time when a thorough investigation into the whole question of radio in Canada should be instituted, and I suggest that a royal commission should be set up to investigate the situation.
In my view, the C.B.C. has a definite role to play* I should not like to see it removed, and I do not criticize it for wanting to play its role-if it would only do so. But I see no reason why it should be allowed to pick off the ripe plums which have been cared for and nurtured by the private stations, just for the purpose of obtaining commercial revenue and a ready-made audience.
The C.A.B. was criticized because of the campaign it lodged recently. Some members of the committee thought it should not have taken that action. I am wondering whether this is another interference with free speech, or if those stations will be under threat of cancellation of their licences if they continue to launch campaigns in which they seek to obtain the rights which they believe they ought to have, and rights which over fifty per cent of the people of Canada think they should have.
Then, the matter of having two ministers has been discussed. The statement is made in the evidence time after time that the C.B.C. is independent of the government. I do not believe it is. If it is independent of the government, why does it need a minister? If it is independent a minister would have nothing to do with it; so why does it require a minister? I do not think it does-unless the government makes its policy. And it is my view that that is what happens. I believe the government has a finger in the pie. and I would not be at all surprised to find that it had a finger in the pie in connection with the matter of granting private licences.
Radio has two ministers. An effort is being made to have two ways of collecting money; first of all. from licence fees and, second, from the consolidated revenue fund. That would seem to be in line with the policy of having two ministers. I suppose some things will be done by the Department of Transport under the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and some by the Minister

Canadian Broadcasting Act
of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), and that is why we have the two ministers. I say there should be only one, or that, conversely, the C.B.C. should be stripped of its regulatory powers, its licensing powers and its powers to make recommendations for licensing.
It should be simply an operating company, and should be made to look after its own knitting and do a better job of broadcasting. Possibly it should be allowed to do experimental and research work, just as the private stations would do, if they were allowed. However, up until recently they were refused that privilege.
The C.B.C. is supposed to operate for the benefit of the listening public, but I say there has been too much parentalism in connection with its operations, something which should be outside its scope altogether. It should not be in a position to say whether it is a good thing for the public to have one kind of radio set or another kind.
In the report the most important people have been overlooked. Those who should have been primarily considered are the listening public, the great masses of the people who do not belong to any organization, federation, society or chamber of commerce. Those are the people who should have been considered. The views of organizations should be respected to a certain extent, as listeners; but what would be best for the great masses of the people, those who must remain silent in this matter, has been forgotten in the report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon.
member's time has expired.

I can finish in a
moment. In Ontario and Quebec we get all the radio entertainment we require, and if we do not like what we get we can turn our dials, and turn off those programmes.
In closing, I should like to read an excerpt from the brief presented by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, which states my views as follows:
To sum up; radio legislation, which has grown up haphazard, needs complete revision. The revision should be made in the light of our past experience and present knowledge; the revision should recognize the potentialities of radio and the essentiality of providing that it be free from interference and even the threat of interference, while subject to necessary regulation.
In such a revision recognition should be given to the fact that there has grown up in Canada not one national system of broadcasting but two separate and competing systems and each should be accorded its proper and rightful place in which it can fully serve the people of Canada.
It is desirable, in the interest of all our people, of all political parties, that so great a power should be removed from even the possibility of political control and should be given a charter under which it can expand, prosper and serve. .
To conclude:
For the reasons given we urge that the public interest requires-
1.	The firm establishment of the legal right to freedom of expression on radio similar to the legal right to freedom of expression in print.
2.	An independent radio licensing and regulating body appointed directly by. financed by and responsible directly to parliament with power to license and regulate all radio in Canada.
Any board of this kind would, of necessity, take evidence from the transport board and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Mr. II. G. ARCHIBALD (Skeena): Mr. Speaker, I shall try to confine myself to quality rather than quantity. The C.B.C. has been referred to quite often in the debate this afternoon as a monopoly, but the opposition to the C.B.C. seems to be in a healthy financial position. There are many' private concerns in this country who would like to be able to put out the balance sheets published by these private radio stations. The argument was advanced this afternoon that a separate regulatory body should be set up over and above the C.B.C. That idea was expressed first by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), who stated that would be far better than the present set-up. He said that there was no argument which could be advanced against that.
There is in this country one institution which would compare with that idealistic body of which he was speaking. I believe this is called the railroad commission. They act like Mussolini; they compel the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National to run their trains at the same time, when it is a well known fact that the Canadian National can get across this continent much faster than the Canadian Pacific. If the C.B.C. allowed itself to get into a jack-pot like that, it would be just the same as any other greenhorn in a tinhorn gambling game.
The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) pointed out that the government could not compete with private enterprise when it came to administering any institution. I notice that when private enterprise gets into financial difficulties it comes weeping and crawling on its hands and knees for help from the state and the government which it condemns.
We want to see the C.B.C. grow through the north country. We criticize them because we cannot get enough. The people in the urban centres contend that the C.B.C. should not operate stations in the large centres. If they were allowed to operate only in the north country, what a howl one would hear when they presented their statement from the so-
Canadian Broadcasting Act

called saviours of the taxpayers. They should be permitted to get some of the cream, so that they can give more service to the remote sections of the country.
In the central part of British Columbia we cannot get enough Canadian radio programmes. There are pockets in the mountainous regions where radio reception is very poor. We would like to have more booster stations established. Boards of trade and other organizations throughout that north country have demanded more service from the C.B.C. I hate to see people who are living off the dividends they receive from gold mines away up in the north sabotaging the people who live there from getting decent radio reception, I say to the C.B.C.: Long may your chimney smoke.

Mr. Speaker, I was not a member of the radio committee, but I wish to say a few words as an ordinary member of the Canadian public and as a radio listener. I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) and others who have spoken in agreement with them. As I say, I wish to speak merely as a member of the Canadian radio listening public.
My opinion is and always has been that the chief purpose of radio is to amuse, to entertain and to give factual news, not to educate the public or try to educate the public or to miseducate the public. It should leave propaganda to recognized spokesmen of the various political parties or movements.
I should like to go back to 1945 when radio time was allotted to the different parties. The Social Credit party was then allotted the same amount of time on the radio as the communist party. At that time the social credit-ers had a dozen members in this House of Commons; there had been a Social Credit government in Alberta since 1935, and they had organizations throughout the rest of the provinces. The communist party had, I think, two members in the house, one of whom is now in prison. They had no provincial government, and they have not had any since. Yet they were given the same amount of time as the social crediters. I contend that this indicates that there is communist socialist control of radio in this country, and that that has been so from the start.
I have not the time to go into the matter fully, but I have made a few investigations of some of the propagandists or employees of the C.B.C. I would refer, first, to Richard Stanton Lambert. He was president of the writers,

artists, broadcasters war council. He arrived from England in 1938 after having been on the staff of the B.B.C. He was C.B.C. supervisor of school broadcasts and chief adviser on talks to C.B.C. He was counsellor of the Toronto civil liberties league and has publicly encouraged subscriptions to the Canadian Tribune. In 1942 he was chairman of a meeting for Anna Louise Strong and assured the meeting that it -would never do to return to the outmoded democratic society of 1939. He always supported lifting the ban on the communist party.
Then there was Raymond Arthur Davies, whose real name is Divinski. Davies is prominent in communist circles in this country which describe him as "popular leader of Young Communist League", "recruiting agent for Young Communist League". In 1938 he edited the communist paper New Advance. In 1939 he was a teacher at the Young Communist school in Toronto. He worked on the Daily Clarion and retains full party membership. In 1940 he was made secretary of the national council of the Y.M.C.A. and secretary of the Canadian Institute of Economics and Politics. Since a visit to Russia, he has written a number of articles for Saturday Night. He formed the writers, authors, artists, broadcasters war council. He left for Russia in October. 1943. The C.B.C. refers to him as Canadian correspondent in the Soviet Union and C.B.C. correspondent Raymond Arthur Davies. I sometimes wonder who finances these people. The Lambert-cum-Davies alliance with C.B.C. and writers, artists, broadcasters war council, plus the fact that Davies is featured as Moscow correspondent of C.B.C. only after Lambert came on the staff of C.B.C. show that Lambert is a communist actively working for the communist party. Those are facts and I can prove them to any person interested enough to look into them.
I could go on, but I think I have said enough to show the danger of propaganda by C.B.C. and by men who have no responsibility, or at least who are not openly responsible to any political movement in this country'. It is all right when the leader of any recognized party or recognized movement in this country' broade casts and is introduced to the public as Mr. So-and-so, the leader of such-and-such a party or movement. That is one thing. The people know who he is and for whom he is speaking. But many' of these commentators, in fact all of them, so far as we are told, have no connection with any' political organization in Canada, and some people naturally think these commentators are actually speaking for the government or purely for disinterested purposes.

Canadian Broadcasting Act
I might mention two men who have certainly done their level best to wean away the loyalty of the Canadian people by selling communism to them. I refer to Elmore Philpott and Matthew Halton. I happen to come from the same country that Matthew Halton does, and I know that those who know him will admit that he is a communist. Yet he is given the free run of the air over C.B.C., while social crediters as such are banned from it or appear under great handicaps.
That shows some wisdom anyway.
It does, of course, to the communist people and to their fellow travellers who make up the bulk of the C.C.F. party.
Including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

After the secret session we
attended last Tuesday, we had, I think, warning enough of the dangers of softening up the people of this country and of other countries to the ideologies of communism, if I understood the speaker and I listened very carefully-

Mr. Speaker, I shall take a few minutes only to speak on radio as it applies to a section of my area, in the north of the province of Quebec. Our private radio stations in Rouyn, Amos and Val d'Or broadcast, at different times, the French programmes of the C.B.C. and there are instances, in the Temisca-mingue and La Sarre-Makamick areas, where our citizens cannot possibly receive the programmes originating from the C.B.C. stations. This situation could certainly be remedied by increasing the power of the private stations in the north country; this would require helping the owners to secure the equipment necessary for increasing power of their transmitters so as to be in a position to cover the whole district, thereby giving a satisfactory service.
Representations have come from some of these areas for five, six and even ten years, requesting fair treatment in this connection. It is therefore a matter of urgency that a solution be found that will satisfy these people.
Now a few words only on the broadcasting periods allotted the Social Credit all through Canada and especially in the province of Quebec. Since broadcasting time is allotted the various political groups, we have had one-quarter of an hour each three or four months. Two fifteen-minute broadcasts in four months for the Union of Electors, in the province of Quebec, are decidedly not enough.
For my part, even if we are told that the blame goes to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which allots those fifteen-minute broadcasting periods, I hold the government responsible as regards the time allotted to the Social Credit group. If, after the next general election, only two or three or even four Liberals are elected throughout Canada, I wonder if the Liberal party will be quite satisfied bo have a quarter of an hour for broadcasting
Canadian Broadcasting Act

every four or five months. The golden rule should never be departed from; therefore, I ask that justice be done to the Union of Electors and all other groups, and that several fifteen-minute broadcasting periods be alloted to us so that we may freely expound our principles throughout Canada. We advocate not slavery, but freedom. We want to be allowed to voice our opinions freely and sincerely over the radio and to organize in our own way our propaganda in accordance with the wishes of our French and English-speaking fellow-citizens.

On this occasion, speaking on a bill of such importance, and particularly as it is the only opportunity we have had to discuss the whole question of radio broadcasting and the constitution of the C.B.C., I regret I shall be unable to finish by six o'clock. I want to say at the outset that for several reasons I am opposed to this bill, the result of which will go to increase the amount handed over to the C.B.C. by over $500,000. The first reason, is that at this time, when our tax rate is already so high and when it is so important to reduce the burden on our people, I am opposed to a measure which will increase the expenditures and will, therefore, increase taxation, without giving a corresponding sendee or result to the people of Canada. If this were simply a question of giving extra revenue to the C.B.C., and it could1 be done without increasing the direct financial burden on the people, then certainly it should not 'be opposed, because in the committee I think a clearly convincing case was made out for the desirability of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation getting increased revenue. But when it is done in this way, in a measure which looks on the surface as though there would be no increased burden, but when actually what is happening or would happen under this measure would be that the people themselves would have to bear the costs of collecting the licences and would have to put up over $500,000, I am opposed to it. My opposition is made stronger because, as was pointed out by an hon. member earlier this afternoon, it means that both those who have radios and those who do not pay licence fees at all will have to pay the extra taxes, since this money can only come out of the consolidated revenue fund of the country. This means that all the taxpayers, not only the radio owners, will be bearing a share of this burden.
There is an additional reason why I am opposed' to this measure. I think the con-

stitution of the body which controls radio in this country should be fully investigated and extensively changed. Therefore I am opposed to paying over $500,000 to an organization whose set-up I do not approve, in so far as my constituents are concerned at any rate. If the constitution of the C.B.C. were changed and the control of radio in Canada put on a proper footing, then the corporation would be in a much better position to come to parliament and ask for more money. To register the protest which I think should be registered on behalf of those whom I represent, I am going to oppose this bill.
The reasons why I am opposed to the present constitution of the C.B.C. and, therefore, why I am opposed to the granting of this money, have already been discussed in the speeches made earlier this afternoon; but I should like to indicate the three main weaknesses, as I see them, in the present situation. First, there is no doubt that the C.B.C. is in competition with private radio, yet under the present Radio Act and the regulations which govern radio in the country the C.B.C.-chiefly the chairman of the board of governors and the board of governors itself-is made judge and jury on any question of conflict which arises between the government-controlled network and the private stations.
May I say here, before going any farther, that my position is not that there should be an end to government control of radio in Canada. It is exactly the opposite. Government control of radio should be made effective and should be removed from the sphere of political controversy. I feel-and I shall give my reasons to substantiate that feeling- that it is not at present out of the field of political controversy, and that to continue the present set-up will only continue a situation in which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation cannot help but be influenced by government policy quite apart from the field of radio, and reflect that political influence in its dealings with other radio broadcasting concerns. That very set-up weakens the whole structure of government control of radio.
What I should like to see is government control of radio, but on a proper basis, a basis in which the people of Canada through their parliament will enact afresh the principles which they wish to govern radio broadcasting in this country, and then to entrust the supervision and the enforcement of these laws to a body independent of the C.B.C. and of the private stations. If that were done, then the objections which are to be found at present to the giving of public moneys to the C.B.C. would be largely removed. I wanted

Canadian Broadcasting Act
to make that clear before going any farther. The position we take is not that government control of radio or even a publicly owned network should be removed and the whole thing be handed back to private interests. The propaganda which has gone out recently, since the radio committeee met this session, has sought to represent that both the Canadian Association of Broadcasters and those who appear to favour this view, are trying to put an end to government control of radio and hand the whole field back to private interests. That, of course, is not the case. At no time in their brief presented to the committee or in their advertising which was inserted in the daily newspapers did the Canadian Association of Broadcasters suggest that government control of radio should end. Indeed, I would say that some of the attacks which have been made on the Canadian Association of Broadcasters' brief, and upon the members of the official opposition taking the position I have just outlined, are deliberate distortions of what are the facts. In his remarks this afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) stated, in effect, that the Canadian Association of Broadcasters and those who agree with them were trying to put an end to government control of broadcasting and were attacking the C.B.C., trying to destroy the C.B.C. and its work. That, of course, is not in accordance with the facts. The C.A.B. never at any time attacked the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation either in the committee or in its advertising campaign. What they did attack was the regulations and the present set-up which, as they pointed out. have in them tremendous capabilities of abuse and potential danger. That was what they were attacking. They did not allege that the C.B.C. is at present abusing its power. In fact this year they were so careful to make their position clear that they did not even attack the policy of the C.B.C. in taking over the frequencies now enjoyed by the three private stations. They accepted that as a matter of C.B.C. policy. It is not quite fair to say that they were thinking of nothing but their vested interests. They see-and I certainly agree with them-a potential danger in the continuation of the method under which control of radio is exercised, and they wanted to improve that.
My second objection to the present set-up of radio in Canada is the apparent confusion in the role of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself. I realize that at the time when public control of broadcasting was first instituted in the country conditions were not as they are now. so that it is not. proper to blame anyone for not having foreseen what would
be the present state of affairs. The position we have arrived at, however, is that the C.B.C. is both a regulating and an operating body, and the one function cannot help detracting from the other. We are in the position now where there is obviously room for both a publicly owned network and privately owned stations, and I have not yet heard anyone suggest-I do not think anyone would be likely to suggest-that privately owned stations should cease to operate and that we should not have any more such stations. That being the fact, it seems to me that it is not logical, it is not in keeping with the way in which we do things in this country, to have one body both operate its own network and regulate other stations which, on occasion, come into competition with it.
My third objection is that the C.B.C. is subject at the moment to political influence; and especially in view of the situation I have described where it both regulates its competitor and operates its own network, that is an undesirable situation and one that shouldi be ended. There are tremendous possibilities of abuse, for instance, in the fact that there are three separate departments all interested and taking their share in the control of radio. The Department of National Revenue, through its minister, in entrusted with the actual supervision of the C.B.C., and with responsibility for the actions of the board of governors. The Department of Transport, through its communications branch, has separate responsibility for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and allocation of frequencies in Canada. In turn, supervision over that branch is in part entrusted to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. So that when you have three ministers each with a finger in the pie you have an opportunity for misunderstanding and confusion and, moreover, you have also a multiplication of opportunities for political interference.
